title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.

TuxBot v3 C2 beacon to Keksec botnet IPs on ports 1999/31337 AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound TCP to the seven hardcoded TuxBot/Keksec C2 IPs, and any public egress to the encrypted-command-dispatch ports 1999/31337 the Go C2 server listens on. Article-specific: pairs named C2 infrastructure with the botnet's distinctive command ports. Rationale: Uses the seven article IP IOCs plus the Go C2 server's documented encrypted-dispatch ports 1999/31337. Port 1999/31337 was independently confirmed by Unit 42 and reflects the multiplexed bot/admin protocol. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://www.netscout.com/blog/asert/asert-threat-summary-aisuru-and-related-turbomirai-botnet-ddos
ATT&CKT1571 T1071 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running external port-scan validation against these ports
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or honeypot infrastructure deliberately touching known-bad IPs
  • A legitimate application coincidentally using ephemeral service on port 1999 (e.g. some game/DB dev tools) to an internal host — excluded by RFC1918 filter
  • Penetration-test C2 emulation using port 31337 as a red-team homage
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nessusd","scanner","masscan") and RemoteIPType == "Public")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the source host (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine); if it is an ELF in /tmp, /dev/shm or a masqueraded name, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network, block all seven C2 IPs and ports 1999/31337 at the egress firewall, and snapshot the binary for hashing. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for the other TuxBot behaviours — DNS to the C2 domains, outbound Telnet/SSH/ADB scanning fan-out, and systemd/cron persistence writes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("209.182.237.133","185.10.68.127","194.46.59.169","45.145.185.229","107.174.133.119","37.32.24.195","154.6.197.43")
   or (RemoteIPType == "Public" and RemotePort in (1999, 31337))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("209.182.237.133","185.10.68.127","194.46.59.169","45.145.185.229","107.174.133.119","37.32.24.195","154.6.197.43")
   or (DstPortNumber in (1999, 31337) and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DvcHostname
| order by ConnCount desc

TuxBot v3 DNS resolution / DNS-TXT C2 to Keksec domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups for the TuxBot C2 domains, including DNS-TXT queries which TuxBot uses as a fallback C2 channel (matching AISURU's TXT-record C2 tradecraft). Article-specific: named domains plus the botnet's documented DNS-TXT command channel. Rationale: Uses the five article domain IOCs and flags the DNS-TXT record type, which is TuxBot's documented fallback C2 mechanism and mirrors AISURU's TXT-record C2 tradecraft (NETSCOUT/Protos). Datadog left empty: DNS-query telemetry has no documented standard source field in this tenant's Datadog schema. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://www.protoslabs.io/resources/aisuru-botnet-deep-dive
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568.002 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate traffic to jetross.com if it resolves to a benign business service (lowest-fidelity of the five domains)
  • Passive DNS / TI enrichment tooling resolving these domains for research
  • Sandbox or malware-analysis VM detonating a sample and generating the lookups
  • Security web proxy pre-fetching/expanding the domains for categorization
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense","MsMpEng.exe","smartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is not a browser/AV-updater and check whether the query type was TXT (strong C2 signal). 2) Contain: sinkhole the domains at internal DNS, isolate the querying host, and block the resolved IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/subnet for TCP beacons to the C2 IPs on 1999/31337 and outbound Telnet/SSH/ADB scanning to confirm full TuxBot infection.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("digikalas.online","cfcybernews.eu","captcha.kanfetka.site","jetross.com","tuxbot.local")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Name has_any ("digikalas.online","cfcybernews.eu","captcha.kanfetka.site","jetross.com","tuxbot.local")
| extend IsTxtC2 = QueryTypeName == "TXT"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryTypeName, IsTxtC2
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IoT/host mass-scan fan-out on Telnet/SSH/ADB from single source (TuxBot scanner) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects the TuxBot propagation scanner: one host opening connections to 100+ distinct destinations on Telnet (23/2323), SSH (22) and Android Debug Bridge (5555) within a short window — the botnet's brute-force/exploit spread behaviour. Article-specific: targets the exact scanner ports and 1,496-credential Telnet brute-force propagation described. Rationale: Targets the article's named scanner protocols (Telnet, SSH, HTTP and ADB) with the 128-concurrent-connection HTTP scanner and 1,496-pair Telnet brute-force as the behavioural signature. The 100-distinct-destination fan-out in 10m separates worm-like spread from admin activity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1046 T1110.001 T1595.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) sweeping the estate
  • Network monitoring / asset-discovery tools doing SSH/Telnet reachability checks
  • A jump host or CI runner legitimately SSHing to a large fleet during deployment
  • Shodan-style external research scanners if the source is internet-facing infra
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nmap","masscan","zmap","nessusd","nuclei","fping")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is a device/server that has no business initiating outbound Telnet/ADB, and identify the scanning process. 2) Contain: quarantine the host, block outbound 23/2323/5555 at egress, and rotate any Telnet/SSH credentials reachable from it. 3) Hunt: check whether the scanning host also beacons to the TuxBot C2 IPs/domains and whether any scanned internal targets subsequently spawned dropped ELF binaries (successful brute-force).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (23, 2323, 5555, 22)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctDests=dcount(RemoteIP), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctDests > 100   // 100+ distinct hosts on Telnet/SSH/ADB ports in 10m = mass scanning, not admin
| order by DistinctDests desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (23, 2323, 5555, 22)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| summarize DistinctDests=dcount(DstIpAddr), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber) by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctDests > 100
| order by DistinctDests desc

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemotePort=/^(23|2323|5555|22)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemotePort], function=count(RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctDests))
| DistinctDests > 100
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs

| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_dests from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555,22) by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_port _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_dests > 100 | sort - distinct_dests
Execution/drop of known TuxBot v3 ELF sample by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on execution or file-write of any of the 20 TuxBot v3 sample hashes disclosed by Unit 42 (cross-compiled ELF bot agents for ARM/MIPS/x86_64/PowerPC/RISC-V). Highest-fidelity host detection — direct known-bad hash match. Rationale: Direct match on the 20 SHA256 sample hashes disclosed by Unit 42; hash IOCs are the highest-fidelity signal in the article. Datadog left empty because Sysmon @Hashes emits uppercase-hex and reliable coverage requires a pipeline lowercase remapper rather than a brittle inline match. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst intentionally detonating a retained sample on a lab host
  • AV/EDR restoring a quarantined copy triggering a file-read event on the hash
  • Threat-hunt tooling hashing files on disk during a sweep (file-read, not execution)
  • Sandbox/CI detonation ranges configured to run submitted binaries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the event is an execution (not an AV quarantine read) and capture the parent process and full path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and add all 20 hashes to the EDR block list. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same hashes and pivot the infected host onto the C2/DNS/scanner detections to scope persistence (systemd/cron) and lateral spread.

TuxBot v3 Linux persistence via systemd/cron written by /tmp-dropped process AIInstallation Medium
Detects the TuxBot persistence routine: a binary running from /tmp, /dev/shm or /var/tmp (or fetched via wget/curl/busybox) that writes a systemd service, cron entry or init.d script — the botnet's documented systemd+cron+watchdog persistence chain. Article-specific: ties the persistence file location to an untrusted execution origin. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact persistence mechanisms (systemd service + cron entries + watchdog) and raises fidelity by requiring the writing process to originate from a transient dir or downloader, which is how a dropped Mirai-lineage ELF installs itself. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/enemybot-a-look-into-keksecs-latest-ddos-botnet
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration-management agents (Ansible/Chef/Puppet) staging units from a temp working dir
  • Package post-install scripts unpacked to /tmp writing systemd units
  • Container/VM provisioning scripts using curl|bash bootstrap patterns
  • Developer/admin manually testing a systemd unit built in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","chef-client","puppet","cloud-init","dpkg","rpm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the created unit/cron file contents and the writing process command line; a reference to a /tmp or randomly-named ELF plus a watchdog respawn loop confirms TuxBot. 2) Contain: disable and remove the systemd service and cron entry, kill the watchdog process, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: hash the referenced binary against the TuxBot sample list, and check the host for C2 beacons and outbound Telnet/SSH/ADB scanning.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/", "/etc/cron.d/", "/etc/cron.hourly/", "/var/spool/cron/", "/etc/init.d/")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/", "/dev/shm/", "/var/tmp/") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wget","curl","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/", "/etc/cron.d/", "/etc/cron.hourly/", "/var/spool/cron/", "/etc/init.d/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/tmp/", "/dev/shm/", "/var/tmp/", "wget", "curl", "busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TuxBot v3 Linux Persistence via systemd/cron from Untrusted Process
id: c5e9f2a7-8b31-4d62-a90c-3d7e1b6c8f05
description: Detects creation of systemd/cron/init.d persistence files by a process executing from /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp or a downloader.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1543.002
  - attack.t1053.003
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
      - '/etc/cron.d/'
      - '/etc/cron.hourly/'
      - '/var/spool/cron/'
      - '/etc/init.d/'
  selection_origin:
    Image|contains:
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - '/var/tmp/'
      - 'wget'
      - 'curl'
      - 'busybox'
  condition: selection_path and selection_origin
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*systemctl\ enable* OR *crontab* OR *"/etc/systemd/system"* OR *"/etc/cron"*) (@process.executable.path:/tmp/* OR @process.executable.path:/dev/shm/* OR @process.executable.path:/var/tmp/* OR @process.name:(wget OR curl OR busybox))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\/(etc\/systemd\/system|etc\/cron\.[a-z]+|var\/spool\/cron|etc\/init\.d)\//i
| (ContextImageFileName=/\/(tmp|dev\/shm|var\/tmp)\// OR ContextImageFileName=/(wget|curl|busybox)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created (Filesystem.file_path="/etc/systemd/system/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.d/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.hourly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/spool/cron/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/init.d/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(process_name,"%/tmp/%") OR like(process_name,"%/dev/shm/%") OR like(process_name,"%/var/tmp/%") OR process_name IN ("wget","curl","busybox") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created (Filesystem.file_path="/etc/systemd/system/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.d/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.hourly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/spool/cron/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/init.d/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(process_name,"%/tmp/%") OR like(process_name,"%/dev/shm/%") OR like(process_name,"%/var/tmp/%") OR process_name IN ("wget","curl","busybox") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

let BadDomains = dynamic(["digikalas.online", "jetross.com", "cfcybernews.eu", "captcha.kanfetka.site", "c2.tuxbot.local"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2013-7471", "CVE-2014-2321", "CVE-2014-8361", "CVE-2017-17215", "CVE-2017-18377", "CVE-2018-10561", "CVE-2018-10562", "CVE-2018-20062", "CVE-2020-17456", "CVE-2022-30525", "CVE-2023-39780", "CVE-2025-34037", "CVE-2026-5815", "CVE-2007-3010", "CVE-2007-5693", "CVE-2016-11021", "CVE-2020-8515", "CVE-2021-4045", "CVE-2021-25646", "CVE-2022-1388", "CVE-2022-22947", "CVE-2022-22965", "CVE-2022-44877", "CVE-2023-1389", "CVE-2025-34117")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2013-7471", "CVE-2014-2321", "CVE-2014-8361", "CVE-2017-17215", "CVE-2017-18377", "CVE-2018-10561", "CVE-2018-10562", "CVE-2018-20062", "CVE-2020-17456", "CVE-2022-30525", "CVE-2023-39780", "CVE-2025-34037", "CVE-2026-5815", "CVE-2007-3010", "CVE-2007-5693", "CVE-2016-11021", "CVE-2020-8515", "CVE-2021-4045", "CVE-2021-25646", "CVE-2022-1388", "CVE-2022-22947", "CVE-2022-22965", "CVE-2022-44877", "CVE-2023-1389", "CVE-2025-34117")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Unauthenticated access to MantisBT admin/install.php on a production host (CVE-2026-52847) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Credential-phishing form injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) · [LLM] Meta open-redirect injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Broad reflected HTML/XSS payload tokens in MantisBT install.php query string · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Unauthenticated access to MantisBT admin/install.php on a production host (CVE-2026-52847) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts for HTTP requests that reach /admin/install.php with a 200 response after deployment. The installer should be removed/restricted post-install; its continued reachability is both the precondition for the reflected-XSS chain and a recon signal. Rationale: Uses the exact installer path /admin/install.php named in the advisory plus a 200-status filter; the installer's reachability is the stated precondition for the whole XSS chain and the workaround is to remove /admin. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory DB entry for CVE-2026-52847. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52847/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin performing an in-place upgrade or fresh install of MantisBT
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring configured to hit the app root that redirects into the installer
  • DevOps CI pipeline validating a freshly deployed MantisBT container
  • Security team running an authorized pentest against the tracker
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8") and csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "Qualys"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the source IP is not an authorized admin/scanner and whether the MantisBT version is <=2.28.3. Review the csUriQuery values returned for injected HTML tokens (form/meta). Step 2 (contain): Remove or ACL-restrict the /admin directory per the vendor workaround, or upgrade to 2.28.4+; block external access to /admin/install.php at the WAF/reverse proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same source IP across web logs for other admin-path probing and for follow-on requests carrying reflected-XSS payloads (see the form-injection and meta-redirect UCs).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where scStatus == 200
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Queries = make_set(csUriQuery, 20) by cIP, csUriStem, csMethod, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by Hits desc
title: MantisBT installer (admin/install.php) reachable post-deployment
id: 6b1f2c94-2d3e-4a71-9d0b-0a7c1e5f9a10
description: Detects successful HTTP access to MantisBT /admin/install.php, which should be removed after installation (CVE-2026-52847 / CVE-2026-52881 precondition).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52847/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1595.002
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|endswith: '/admin/install.php'
    sc-status: 200
  condition: selection
level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/admin/install.php" Web.status=200 by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path Web.http_method Web.status Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/admin/install.php" Web.status=200 by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path Web.http_method Web.status Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
Credential-phishing form injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) AIDelivery High
Detects HTTP requests to /admin/install.php whose query string carries injected <form>/action markup — the credential-phishing primitive the advisory calls out, enabled by the missing CSP form-action directive. The payload is reflected from user-supplied parameters via print_test_result(). Rationale: Targets the advisory's explicit 'credential-phishing form injection' primitive using the concrete injector path /admin/install.php and injected <form action=...> tokens (both raw and URL-encoded). The missing form-action CSP directive means the injected form is the actual exploitation vector, making these tokens high-fidelity. Confirmed via GitLab CVE-2026-52881 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1189 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentester/bug-bounty tester replaying the watchTowr PoC against the tracker
  • A generic web vulnerability scanner (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) firing XSS templates that include <form> payloads
  • A legitimate query parameter that coincidentally contains the literal string 'action=http' (e.g. a callback/return URL param)
  • WAF audit-mode traffic replaying attack corpora
Suppression filter
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<form", "%3Cform", "formaction") // require an actual form tag, not just action=http return-URL params
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the csUriQuery and confirm an injected <form> with an action pointing off-host; note the target action domain as attacker credential-harvest infra. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP and the harvest domain at the WAF/proxy, and restrict/remove /admin/install.php or upgrade to MantisBT 2.28.4+. Step 3 (hunt): Search web logs for any admin sessions or credential POSTs to the identified harvest domain, and pivot on the source IP for the meta-redirect variant and installer-probe activity.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<form", "%3Cform", "formaction", "form%20action", "action=http", "action%3Dhttp", "method=post", "method%3Dpost")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csMethod, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Meta open-redirect injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) AIDelivery High
Detects requests to /admin/install.php whose reflected query string contains injected <meta http-equiv=refresh> markup — the open-redirect primitive the advisory describes, also enabled by the absent CSP form-action directive. Redirects victims silently to phishing/malware. Rationale: Targets the advisory's explicit '<meta> open redirects' primitive, requiring both an injected <meta> token and a refresh/http-equiv/url= token on the exact /admin/install.php path so it fires only on the redirect-injection shape, not generic meta references. Confirmed via GitLab CVE-2026-52881 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentester replaying the watchTowr open-redirect PoC
  • Automated scanner (Nuclei/ZAP) firing open-redirect templates containing <meta refresh>
  • A legitimate parameter carrying a 'url=http...' return address that coincidentally sits near a meta reference
  • WAF corpus replay in audit mode
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode csUriQuery, extract the redirect target URL from the injected <meta ... url=> and check it against threat intel. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP and redirect-target domain at the WAF/proxy; remove/restrict /admin/install.php or upgrade to 2.28.4+. Step 3 (hunt): Look for users who subsequently connected to the redirect-target domain (proxy/DNS logs) and correlate with the same source IP's form-injection or probe activity.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<meta", "%3Cmeta")
| where csUriQuery has_any ("http-equiv", "refresh", "url=http", "url%3Dhttp")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csMethod, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Broad reflected HTML/XSS payload tokens in MantisBT install.php query string AIExploitation Medium
Hunting-tier catch-all for any HTML-injection markup reflected through /admin/install.php's six unescaped print_test_result() parameters. Broader than the targeted form/meta rules — surfaces CSS-injection UI-manipulation and event-handler probing that the tighter alerting rules miss. Rationale: Ties any HTML-markup token to the specific vulnerable path /admin/install.php named in the advisory; scoping the broad angle-bracket/event-handler net to this one endpoint keeps it deployable while catching CSS-injection UI manipulation and probing the two alerting rules don't cover. The endpoint anchor is what makes this article-specific rather than a generic WAF signature. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52847/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated web scanners (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) sweeping the endpoint with XSS payloads
  • Authorized pentest of the tracker
  • A benign query parameter containing a literal '<' or 'javascript:' substring in a URL value
  • WAF/IDS test traffic replaying attack corpora against the app
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "Qualys" and csUserAgent !has "Nuclei" and csUserAgent !has "zgrab"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Group by source IP and inspect the make_set of reflected payloads to distinguish scanner noise (many varied payloads) from a targeted single-payload exploit; check MantisBT version. Step 2 (contain): If exploitation-grade payloads are present, restrict/remove /admin/install.php or upgrade to 2.28.4+ and block the source IP. Step 3 (hunt): Escalate confirmed hits into the form-injection and meta-redirect UCs, and review whether any admin credentials were entered on the affected page during the window.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<", "%3C", "onerror", "onload", "<style", "%3Cstyle", "<script", "%3Cscript", "javascript:")
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Payloads = make_set(csUriQuery, 25) by cIP, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by Hits desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Google Gemini CLI abused as a hacking agent, malware botnet operator

BleepingComputer
2026-07-15 6 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A Russian-speaking threat actor known as "bandcampro" used Google's open-source Gemini CLI AI tool as a hacking agent and to operate a small-scale botnet. [...]

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1027 T1047 T1053.005 T1059.001 T1190

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] bandcampro Gemini-CLI botnet: PowerShell agent C2 to c2.trialersafe.com · [LLM] PowerShell agent 5-second fixed-interval C2 beacon to public host (bandcampro botnet) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
bandcampro Gemini-CLI botnet: PowerShell agent C2 to c2.trialersafe.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoints resolving or connecting to the botnet's command-and-control host c2.trialersafe.com, the C2 fronted by a Cloudflare tunnel that bandcampro's Gemini-CLI-operated PowerShell agents polled. Article-specific because it pins the exact C2 FQDN and surfaces the initiating process to confirm the lightweight PowerShell agent. Rationale: Pivots on the exact C2 FQDN c2.trialersafe.com pulled from the article's IOC set; projecting InitiatingProcessFileName confirms the PowerShell agent described by Trend Micro. Domain-match on a dedicated 'c2.' subdomain is inherently low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/07/14/the-bots-are-alive-jailbroken-gemini-spun-up-new-c2-server-for-russian-fraudster-in-just-6-minutes/5270131 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/google-gemini-cli-abused-as-a-hacking-agent-malware-botnet-operator/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / red-team replaying the published IOC in a sandbox that shares the org's egress
  • Threat-intel feed validation tooling actively resolving the IOC to confirm it is still live
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS appliance logging the blocked lookup (still worth reviewing which host asked)
  • Typo-adjacent legitimate domain sharing the 'trialersafe' token if a marketing/trial service exists
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source host and the InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine — confirm powershell.exe/pwsh.exe or an in-memory script initiated the lookup/connection versus a browser or DNS security tool. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, block c2.trialersafe.com and its resolved IPs at DNS/proxy/firewall, and kill the offending PowerShell process. Step 3 (hunt): On the isolated host review scheduled tasks, WMI event subscriptions, and Run/RunOnce registry values (the article's three persistence mechanisms), then pivot on the resolved IP and any Cloudflare tunnel endpoints to find sibling bots polling the same C2.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "trialersafe.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "trialersafe.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP, Indicator = Name, Src = "DNS"),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "trialersafe.com" or RequestURL has "trialersafe.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Indicator = coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Src = "Proxy/FW")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Botnet C2 Connection to c2.trialersafe.com (bandcampro Gemini-CLI botnet)
id: 2f3a7c4e-9b1d-4e6a-8c0f-5d2b7a1e9c33
description: Detects DNS resolution or connection to the bandcampro botnet C2 host c2.trialersafe.com operated via Gemini CLI.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/google-gemini-cli-abused-as-a-hacking-agent-malware-botnet-operator/
  - https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/07/14/the-bots-are-alive-jailbroken-gemini-spun-up-new-c2-server-for-russian-fraudster-in-just-6-minutes/5270131
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|contains: 'trialersafe.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*trialersafe.com* OR *TRIALERSAFE.COM*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/trialersafe\.com/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="c2.trialersafe.com" OR All_Traffic.dest="*trialersafe.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="c2.trialersafe.com" OR All_Traffic.dest="*trialersafe.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - count
PowerShell agent 5-second fixed-interval C2 beacon to public host (bandcampro botnet) AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioural detection for the botnet's PowerShell agents that polled the in-memory Python HTTP C2 every five seconds — a tight, regular ~12-connections-per-minute cadence to a public destination. Survives C2 domain/IP rotation because it keys on the beacon regularity from a PowerShell initiator rather than the specific FQDN. Rationale: Keys on the article's explicit '5-second polling' cadence from a PowerShell agent to a public host — a regular ~12/min beacon is distinctive versus human-driven or bursty PowerShell traffic and survives C2 rotation. Sentinel version loses process attribution (no process-attributed network table in this tenant's schema) so it keys on beacon regularity alone. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/07/14/the-bots-are-alive-jailbroken-gemini-spun-up-new-c2-server-for-russian-fraudster-in-just-6-minutes/5270131 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/google-gemini-cli-abused-as-a-hacking-agent-malware-botnet-operator/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.001 T1029
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PowerShell-based monitoring/health-check scripts that poll a SaaS or internal API on a fixed short interval
  • Configuration-management agents (DSC, custom polling wrappers) invoked through powershell.exe
  • PowerShell modules pulling telemetry to Azure/AWS endpoints at a steady cadence
  • Long-running interactive PowerShell session with an open websocket/keepalive to a cloud service
  • Update/license-check scripts that reconnect every few seconds during a sync window
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("Update-","Get-Metric","HealthCheck","Az.","AWSPowerShell","Invoke-DscResource")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain for the beaconing PowerShell — legitimate pollers are usually signed scripts with clear API hostnames, whereas the agent runs in-memory with no script path. Resolve the RemoteIP and check reputation / whether it fronts a Cloudflare tunnel. Step 2 (contain): If unattributed, isolate the host and kill the PowerShell process; block the destination IP/ASN at egress. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for other hosts beaconing to the same IP at the same cadence (the botnet had ~8 nodes), and inspect scheduled tasks, WMI event subscriptions, and Run keys on affected hosts for the agent's persistence.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1m)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| extend DurationMin = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| extend Rate = todouble(ConnCount) / (DurationMin + 1)   // 5s polling => ~12 conn/min
| where DistinctMinutes >= 10 and ConnCount >= 60          // sustained, not a burst
| where Rate >= 6 and Rate <= 20                           // cadence band consistent with a 5s beacon
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| summarize ConnCount = count(), DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| extend DurationMin = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| extend Rate = todouble(ConnCount) / (DurationMin + 1)   // 5s polling => ~12 conn/min
| where DistinctMinutes >= 10 and ConnCount >= 60
| where Rate >= 6 and Rate <= 20
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| count > 60
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(_time) as distinct_secs values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") All_Traffic.dest_category="public" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest _time span=1m | stats sum(count) as ConnCount dc(_time) as DistinctMinutes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest dest_port | eval DurationMin=round((lastTime-firstTime)/60,0), rate=ConnCount/(DurationMin+1) | where DistinctMinutes>=10 AND ConnCount>=60 AND rate>=6 AND rate<=20 | sort - ConnCount
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(_time) as distinct_secs values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") All_Traffic.dest_category="public" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest _time span=1m | stats sum(count) as ConnCount dc(_time) as DistinctMinutes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest dest_port | eval DurationMin=round((lastTime-firstTime)/60,0), rate=ConnCount/(DurationMin+1) | where DistinctMinutes>=10 AND ConnCount>=60 AND rate>=6 AND rate<=20 | sort - ConnCount
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("payloads.tralalarkefe.com", "c2.trailerkeefe.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["payloads.tralalarkefe.com", "c2.trailerkeefe.com"]);
ImNetworkSession

MantisBT CVE-2026-47156: self-registration followed by SOAP API replay from same source IP AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-47156 exploitation chain: a zero-access attacker self-registers (POST to signup.php, enabled by default) then immediately drives the flawed SOAP endpoint (/api/soap/mantisconnect.php) from the same client to replay a cookie_string as the administrator. Correlating a fresh signup with SOAP activity from one IP within a short window is the article-specific fingerprint that a legitimate SOAP integration user would never produce. Rationale: Anchored on the two concrete article paths — signup.php (default-enabled self-registration, the zero-access foothold) and /api/soap/mantisconnect.php (the vulnerable SOAP endpoint, path confirmed via mantisbt.org docs) — correlated on a single SourceIP within a tight window, a sequence a normal SOAP integration client never generates. Cross-checked against: • https://mantisbt.org/blog/archives/mantisbt/852 • https://mantisbt.org/docs/master/en-US/Developers_Guide/html/soapapi.html • https://github.com/mantisbt/mantisbt/commit/e3571c319b1721b41b0dc4b5b5203cbdcbe0c2ee
ATT&CKT1190 T1136.001 T1550.004 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuinely new user self-registers, then a SOAP integration/bot they own begins polling from the same corporate NAT egress IP.
  • Many users behind one proxy/NAT SourceIP: one person registers while an unrelated SOAP integration runs from the same shared IP.
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner or DAST crawling both signup.php and the API surface from a single scan-node IP.
  • CI/QA automation that programmatically registers a test user then exercises the SOAP API against a staging instance.
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (_GetWatchlist('KnownApiClients') | project SearchKey)  // maintain a watchlist of sanctioned SOAP-integration egress IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the SourceIP over the surrounding 24h; confirm the signup.php POST succeeded (2xx) and enumerate which SOAP calls followed. Identify the account created and whether SOAP calls returned admin-scoped data (private projects/issues, user lists). 2) Contain: disable/delete the freshly-registered account, block the SourceIP at the WAF, and force-rotate the administrator's cookie_string/session; confirm MantisBT is upgraded to 2.28.4+ (no workaround exists). 3) Hunt: search for other IPs hitting mantisconnect.php shortly after any signup.php POST, review SOAP mutation/delete operations, and audit for created/modified issues or deleted projects during the window.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let signups = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where RequestURL has "signup.php" and RequestMethod == "POST"
    | project SignupTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where RequestURL has "mantisconnect.php"
| join kind=inner signups on SourceIP
| where TimeGenerated between (SignupTime .. SignupTime + window)
| summarize SoapRequests = count(), FirstSoap = min(TimeGenerated), LastSoap = max(TimeGenerated), SampleUrl = any(RequestURL) by SourceIP, SignupTime
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', FirstSoap, SignupTime)  // signup-to-SOAP gap; exploit is typically minutes
| sort by LastSoap desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="*signup.php" OR Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php") by Web.src, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| stats dc(uri_path) as distinct_endpoints values(uri_path) as endpoints_hit min(first_seen) as first_activity max(last_seen) as last_activity sum(count) as total_requests by src
| where distinct_endpoints>=2
| eval chain_window_minutes=round((last_activity-first_activity)/60,1)
| sort - last_activity
| tstats summariesonly=false count earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="*signup.php" OR Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php") by Web.src, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| stats dc(uri_path) as distinct_endpoints values(uri_path) as endpoints_hit min(first_seen) as first_activity max(last_seen) as last_activity sum(count) as total_requests by src
| where distinct_endpoints>=2
| eval chain_window_minutes=round((last_activity-first_activity)/60,1)
| sort - last_activity
MantisBT SOAP endpoint high-volume request burst (CVE-2026-47156 mass enumeration/exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts post-bypass data theft: once authenticated as administrator over SOAP, the attacker drives the 71 SOAP operations at /api/soap/mantisconnect.php to enumerate and bulk-exfiltrate every issue, attachment, and user-PII record. Because all SOAP operations POST to the same endpoint, a sharp volume burst of POSTs (and outbound bytes) from one client is the detectable signature of automated enumeration disproportionate to normal integration polling. Rationale: Uses the concrete SOAP endpoint path from the article/docs plus a request-rate and outbound-byte burst to model the '71 SOAP operations / full data exfiltration' behaviour; SOAP-operation names live in the POST body (invisible to access logs) so volume + bytes from a single client is the highest-fidelity signal available on this telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://mantisbt.org/docs/master/en-US/Developers_Guide/html/soapapi.html • https://mantisbt.org/blog/archives/mantisbt/846
ATT&CKT1213 T1005 T1567.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned SOAP integration (dashboard/reporting tool, CI/CD, mobile client) performing a legitimate bulk issue sync.
  • Scheduled backup or data-migration job pulling all issues/attachments through the SOAP API.
  • Monitoring/health-check tooling polling mantisconnect.php at high frequency.
  • Multiple API clients aggregated behind one NAT/proxy SourceIP inflating the per-IP count.
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (_GetWatchlist('KnownApiClients') | project SearchKey)  // exclude sanctioned high-volume SOAP integrations
Response runbook
1) Triage: profile the top SourceIP's request rate versus its own 30-day baseline and confirm whether it maps to a known integration; sample response sizes to gauge how much data left. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, block the SourceIP at the WAF and revoke/rotate the administrator cookie_string and API tokens; snapshot logs for scope of exfiltration (issues, attachments, user PII). 3) Hunt: correlate the burst back to a preceding signup.php registration (UC1), check for subsequent destructive SOAP mutations (deleted projects/issues), and confirm the instance is patched to 2.28.4+.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "mantisconnect.php" and RequestMethod == "POST"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), TotalBytesOut = sum(toint(SentBytes)), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where RequestCount > 100   // 100 SOAP POSTs / 10 min far exceeds normal integration polling cadence
| sort by RequestCount desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php" AND Web.http_method="POST" by Web.src, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where count>100
| eval mb_out=round(bytes_out/1024/1024,1)
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php" AND Web.http_method="POST" by Web.src, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where count>100
| eval mb_out=round(bytes_out/1024/1024,1)
| sort - count

Security teams have never had more visibility, yet rarely have they felt more uncertain. Signal pours in from endpoints, identities, cloud workloads, and a sprawling mix of third-party tools.
