Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Service Persistence via sc.exe with User-Writable Path
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0e
status: experimental
description: |
    sc.exe create with the binary path under \Users\, \AppData\,
    \ProgramData\, or \Temp\ — service-install persistence outside
    legitimate program directories.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1543.003
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_sc:
        Image|endswith: '\sc.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: 'create'
    selection_path:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '\Users\'
            - '\AppData\'
            - '\ProgramData\'
            - '\Temp\'
    condition: selection_sc and selection_path
falsepositives:
    - Internal install scripts dropping a service from %ProgramData%
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="sc.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*\Users\*" OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*"
        OR Processes.process="*\ProgramData\*" OR Processes.process="*\Temp\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
        where Registry.registry_path="*\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*"
          AND Registry.registry_value_name="ImagePath"
          AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*\Users\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="sc.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*\Users\*" OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*"
        OR Processes.process="*\ProgramData\*" OR Processes.process="*\Temp\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
        where Registry.registry_path="*\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*"
          AND Registry.registry_value_name="ImagePath"
          AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*\Users\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`]
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious @asyncapi package versions installed via npm/node (AsyncAPI supply-chain) · [LLM] Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS (ipfs.io + campaign CIDs)

Malicious @asyncapi package versions installed via npm/node (AsyncAPI supply-chain) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for installation or CI/CD invocation of the five trojanized @asyncapi package@version strings published during the July 14 2026 exposure window. Article-specific because it pins the exact malicious versions (e.g. @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2) that carry the first-stage IPFS downloader. Rationale: Pins the five exact malicious package@version strings confirmed by Socket, StepSecurity and Wiz; the safe versions (3.3.0/1.1.0/0.7.0/6.11.1) differ so an exact-version match is high fidelity for the poisoned releases. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally reproducing the incident in a sandbox
  • A pinned lockfile install that resolves the version transitively without the version string appearing on the command line (false negative, not FP)
  • Internal mirror/proxy replay of npm audit logs referencing the version for remediation testing
  • CI pipeline pinned to 6.11.1 but with a typo'd tag in a comment/log line
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually resolved the malicious version — inspect package-lock.json / node_modules/@asyncapi/*/package.json for the pinned versions and check install time against the 07:10–11:18 UTC 2026-07-14 window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete node_modules and lockfiles built during the window, and block npm publish/pull to the affected packages. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC for %LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS\sync.js drop and outbound C2 to 85.137.53.71 to confirm second/third-stage detonation, then rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs, SSH keys, AWS/cloud creds on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","bash.exe","sh","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects install/build invocation referencing the exact trojanized @asyncapi package versions published to npm on 2026-07-14.
references:

  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm

Miasma sync.js payload dropped to masqueraded NodeJS app-data folder AIInstallation High
Detects the second/third-stage 'sync.js' loader being written to the OS-specific NodeJS masquerade directory (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS, ~/.config/node). This is the on-disk staging artifact the incident responders are told to delete. Rationale: 'NodeJS\sync.js' is a unique, cross-source-confirmed artifact (Socket + StepSecurity) placed in a folder deliberately named to impersonate legitimate Node.js data; legitimate Node tooling does not write a file named exactly sync.js to these paths. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer project that legitimately contains a src file called sync.js copied into an unrelated NodeJS-named folder (rare)
  • Backup/sync software mirroring an already-infected profile directory to a new host
  • EDR re-scan replaying an old file-create event after remediation
  • Antivirus quarantine restore writing the file back to its original path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture SHA256 of the written sync.js and compare to the reported hashes; identify the InitiatingProcess (expect a detached node.exe). 2) Contain: kill any node process executing sync.js, delete the NodeJS/sync.js file and its parent folder, and network-isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to 85.137.53.71 and Nostr/DHT relays, review persistence (Run keys, crontab, launchd, systemd), and rotate all developer secrets on the machine.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where FolderPath has @"\NodeJS\" or FolderPath has "/NodeJS/" or FolderPath endswith "/.config/node/sync.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "NodeJS" or TargetFilePath endswith "/.config/node/sync.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js executing the hidden Miasma sync.js loader AIExploitation High
Detects a node process whose command line invokes the staged loader at the NodeJS masquerade path (…\NodeJS\sync.js). This is the execution of the detached, hidden (windowsHide:true / stdio:ignore) second-stage that fetches the third-stage Miasma framework. Rationale: Command line referencing the exact staged loader path (…NodeJS\sync.js) run by node is a direct execution signal for the multi-stage loader described by Socket and confirmed by The Hacker News; nearly zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who legitimately named a script sync.js and happens to store it under a folder literally called NodeJS
  • Automated test harness re-running a captured malicious sample in a lab
  • Forensic tooling replaying the process image path during analysis
  • Shell alias or wrapper that echoes the path without executing it (log-only)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sync.js file hash and that the process was spawned detached/hidden (parent is node/npm from the package import). 2) Contain: terminate the node process tree, isolate the host, and delete the NodeJS/sync.js payload. 3) Hunt: correlate with outbound C2 to 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 and Nostr/DHT/Ethereum-RPC egress, enumerate persistence (Run key, crontab, launchd, systemd), and rotate credentials/tokens harvested by Miasma.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"NodeJS\sync.js","NodeJS/sync.js","node/sync.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (@"NodeJS\sync.js","NodeJS/sync.js","node/sync.js") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"NodeJS\sync.js","NodeJS/sync.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma multi-channel C2 egress (85.137.53.71, Nostr, BitTorrent DHT, Ethereum RPC) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections to the Miasma C2 IP 85.137.53.71 (ports 8080/8081/8091) or, when initiated by node, to the campaign's covert channels: Nostr relays, BitTorrent DHT bootstrap nodes, and the public Ethereum RPC used for on-chain C2 addressing. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 with ports 8080/8081/8091 is the unique C2/upload/proxy triple confirmed by StepSecurity and Socket; the Nostr/DHT/Ethereum-RPC domains are the campaign's covert C2 channels and are highly anomalous when initiated by node.exe on a dev/CI host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a legitimate Nostr client or Ethereum dApp that contacts relay.damus.io or ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com (filter requires node initiator to reduce this)
  • A torrent client legitimately bootstrapping via router.bittorrent.com:6881 on a personal machine
  • Blockchain/web3 CI pipeline that legitimately queries publicnode.com RPC
  • Threat-intel/IOC-validation tooling probing the C2 IP from a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe running sync.js) and the destination/port; confirm the host installed a poisoned @asyncapi version. 2) Contain: block 85.137.53.71 and the covert-channel domains at the egress firewall, isolate the host, kill the node C2 process. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for any host beaconing to the same IP/domains, review IPFS retrievals (ipfs.io + the reported CIDs), enumerate persistence, and rotate npm/GitHub/SSH/AWS/cloud credentials harvested by the stealer.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71" and RemotePort in (8080,8081,8091))
     or (RemoteUrl has_any ("relay.damus.io","relay.nostr.com","ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com","router.bittorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71" and DstPortNumber in (8080,8081,8091))
     or DstHostname has_any ("relay.damus.io","relay.nostr.com","ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com","router.bittorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS (ipfs.io + campaign CIDs) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for a node process fetching the encrypted second stage over IPFS — either resolving/contacting ipfs.io or referencing the two campaign content IDs (QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9, Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf). IPFS egress from a Node process on a dev/CI host is highly abnormal. Rationale: ipfs.io is the confirmed delivery gateway (Socket/StepSecurity) and the two Qm… CIDs are the exact content hashes of the generator/specs payloads; pairing the gateway with a node initiator surfaces the ingress-tool-transfer step without over-matching legitimate IPFS use. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm
ATT&CKT1105 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately using an IPFS-backed tool or web3 app that resolves ipfs.io from Node
  • dApp/NFT build pipeline pulling assets from the public IPFS gateway
  • Package manager or CDN that proxies content via ipfs.io
  • Browser-extension helper spawned by node contacting ipfs.io for unrelated content
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sync.js","NodeJS") or RemoteUrl has_any ("QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node process and check whether the URL/path contains the campaign CIDs; correlate timing with a poisoned @asyncapi install. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node processes reaching ipfs.io, and delete any downloaded sync.js. 3) Hunt: check for the follow-on C2 to 85.137.53.71 and covert channels, capture and hash the fetched payload for IOC expansion, and rotate developer secrets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf")
     or (RemoteUrl has "ipfs.io" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "ipfs.io"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:

    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7") or SHA1 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7") or MD5 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7") or SHA1 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7") or MD5 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-07-15 21 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A malware framework called OkoBot has been running on Windows machines since April 2025, and one of its modules is built to con hardware wallet owners out of their recovery phrase. On an infected PC, the request comes from inside the wallet's own desktop software. Sometimes it waits until you plug the device in first. The page is malicious. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OkoBot Malware Framework Injects Seed Phrase Phishing Into Ledger and Trezor App
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OkoBot 'Apple Sync' scheduled task rebuilding reverse SSH tunnel for RDP · [LLM] OkoBot implant staging files (HDUtil.exe, hwid.dat, go.bat, extl.exe) dropped · [LLM] termsrv.dll tampering to enable concurrent RDP sessions · [LLM] Windows Defender notification suppression via registry write · [LLM] Hidden Chromium extension planted via Local Extension Settings (Rilide loader) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse SSH tunnel to OkoBot infrastructure from user endpoint · [LLM] OkoBot C2 beacon to moonsand.store and TookPS/Volume2 infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OkoBot RDP enablement: Remote Desktop Users add + inbound 3389 firewall rule · [LLM] SeedHunter process injection into Ledger/Trezor wallet applications · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
OkoBot 'Apple Sync' scheduled task rebuilding reverse SSH tunnel for RDP AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a scheduled task literally named 'Apple Sync' that OkoBot's TookPS stage registers to rebuild an hourly reverse-SSH tunnel forwarding the local RDP port. The task name is a fixed, article-specific artifact. Rationale: 'Apple Sync' is a hard-coded scheduled-task name confirmed by both THN and Kaspersky's Securelist teardown; it has no legitimate Windows/Apple origin, making name-match near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party sync utility that a vendor coincidentally named 'Apple Sync' (rare)
  • Internal red-team emulation of this exact IOC
  • iTunes/Apple Devices helper tasks (named 'AppleSync'/'MobileDeviceService', not 'Apple Sync' with space + schtasks create)
  • Admin scripting a scheduled task with a demo name during testing
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("itunes.exe","AppleMobileDeviceService.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "ssh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks/Register-ScheduledTask command line and the task XML (schtasks /query /tn 'Apple Sync' /xml) — expect an hourly trigger launching ssh/plink forwarding 3389. 2) Contain: disable+delete the task, kill any ssh.exe/sshd.exe tunnels, isolate the host, and disable exposed local RDP accounts. 3) Hunt: check for %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo\HDUtil.exe, hwid.dat, %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\go.bat, termsrv.dll tampering, and outbound SSH to 104.243.43.16 / 104.243.32.213 / 62.210.188.209.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("create","Apple Sync"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask" and ProcessCommandLine has "Apple Sync")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName has "schtasks.exe" or NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe"))
| where CommandLine has "Apple Sync"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: OkoBot Apple Sync Scheduled Task Creation
id: 3f2a9c1e-6b4d-4a7e-8c2f-1e9d5b7a0c31
description: Detects creation of a scheduled task named 'Apple Sync' used by OkoBot/TookPS to rebuild an hourly reverse SSH tunnel for RDP
references:
  - https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1572
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: 'Apple Sync'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*Apple?Sync* @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\Schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\PWSH.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/Apple Sync/i
| ImageFileName=/(schtasks|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe OR Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) Processes.process="*Apple Sync*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe OR Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) Processes.process="*Apple Sync*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OkoBot implant staging files (HDUtil.exe, hwid.dat, go.bat, extl.exe) dropped AIInstallation Medium
Hunts on-disk drop of OkoBot's fixed staging artifacts and their MD5s: %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo\HDUtil.exe, %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat, %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\go.bat, %PROGRAMDATA%\oko_ver and %TEMP%\extl.exe. These paths/names are unique to this framework. Rationale: File names/paths (%PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo\HDUtil.exe, hwid.dat, .ssh\go.bat, oko_ver, extl.exe) and their MD5s are verbatim from THN and Securelist's IOC table — a name+hash match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated app legitimately writing a generic hwid.dat hardware-ID cache (check path — OkoBot uses %PROGRAMDATA%/%APPDATA%)
  • Developer's own go.bat in a personal .ssh folder (rare; check content)
  • Security tooling copying the samples for analysis on a sandbox host
  • Backup/EDR agent re-materializing quarantined copies
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) and hash-match; benign hwid.dat won't sit under HDVideo alongside HDUtil.exe. 2) Contain: quarantine the files, kill the parent chain, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to the 'Apple Sync' task, outbound SSH to the bot IPs, termsrv.dll modification and the moonsand.store beacon on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\HDVideo\" and FileName =~ "HDUtil.exe")
    or (FolderPath has @"\.ssh\" and FileName =~ "go.bat")
    or FileName =~ "hwid.dat"
    or FileName =~ "oko_ver"
    or FileName =~ "extl.exe"
    or MD5 in~ ("ac93a821617aea1f56d4bc0bef4af327","11dbc8a2bea04b15f8f68f3f01e8faf9","70fef9fd6e351f4d53cfeee8dcdfcd99","3d2b43f91f65bfbf36a9c71b6b418876","dd52f5108a176c62ad807c327734ad12","acd31c9941b6c1cabd4e45e6877b9038")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\HDVideo\" and TargetFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe")
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\.ssh\" and TargetFileName =~ "go.bat")
    or TargetFileName in~ ("hwid.dat","oko_ver","extl.exe")
    or Hash in~ ("ac93a821617aea1f56d4bc0bef4af327","11dbc8a2bea04b15f8f68f3f01e8faf9","70fef9fd6e351f4d53cfeee8dcdfcd99","dd52f5108a176c62ad807c327734ad12","acd31c9941b6c1cabd4e45e6877b9038")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Hash, ActingProcessName
title: OkoBot Framework Staging File Drop
id: 8c1d4e2a-9f7b-4c3d-a6e1-2b5f0d8c9a44
description: Detects OkoBot/TookPS staging artifacts written to disk by fixed name and path
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

termsrv.dll tampering to enable concurrent RDP sessions AIInstallation High
Hunts modification/replacement of C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll by anything other than Windows servicing components — OkoBot swaps in a patched build that permits concurrent RDP sessions to support its hourly reverse-RDP tunnel. Rationale: termsrv.dll is a protected System32 binary normally only touched by TrustedInstaller/servicing; the article explicitly names its replacement for concurrent RDP, so a write by any other process is high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1112 T1543.003 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows cumulative/quality update servicing termsrv.dll (excluded via TrustedInstaller/TiWorker filter)
  • Legitimate 'RDP Wrapper' admin tool an internal team deployed for multi-session RDP
  • Third-party patch-management agent staging a hotfix
  • Antivirus restoring a quarantined original DLL
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "RDPWInst.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the modifying process and compare termsrv.dll hash/signature to the OS-shipped build (sfc /verifyfile). 2) Contain: restore the original DLL, disable concurrent-session patching, isolate host, review active RDP sessions. 3) Hunt: correlate with 'Apple Sync' task, Remote Desktop Users group additions, firewall 3389 rules, and OkoBot staging files on the host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5

OkoBot RDP enablement: Remote Desktop Users add + inbound 3389 firewall rule AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the OkoBot 'build a desk' sequence — adding an account to the Remote Desktop Users group, opening the firewall for inbound RDP (3389), and clearing fDenyTSConnections — from user endpoints. These are the lateral-access primitives the SSH bot sets up post-injection. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'opens the firewall for inbound RDP', 'adds an account to the Remote Desktop Users group', and concurrent-RDP enablement — each maps to a concrete net/netsh/reg command line clustered on one host. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1098 T1562.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/IT enabling RDP + adding a support account for legitimate remote assistance
  • GPO/Intune remediation script opening 3389 on managed hosts
  • Server-build automation setting fDenyTSConnections=0
  • Pentest/red-team RDP enablement
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("IntuneManagementExtension.exe","gpscript.exe","omadmclient.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether all three primitives (group add + firewall + fDenyTS) cluster on one endpoint in a short window and whether the initiating process is a known admin tool. 2) Contain: revert firewall rule, remove the added RDP account, re-set fDenyTSConnections=1, isolate if unexplained. 3) Hunt: pivot to termsrv.dll change, 'Apple Sync' task, and outbound SSH to the OkoBot bot IPs from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and ProcessCommandLine has "add")
    or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "advfirewall" and ProcessCommandLine has "3389")
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("net.exe","net1.exe") and CommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and CommandLine has "add")
    or (NewProcessName has "netsh.exe" and CommandLine has "advfirewall" and CommandLine has "3389")
    or (NewProcessName has "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 ((@Image:(*\net.exe OR *\net1.exe OR *\NET.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*Remote?Desktop?Users* AND @CommandLine:*add*) OR (@Image:(*\netsh.exe OR *\NETSH.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*advfirewall* AND @CommandLine:*3389*) OR (@Image:(*\reg.exe OR *\REG.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*fDenyTSConnections*))

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name IN (net.exe,net1.exe) Processes.process="*Remote Desktop Users*" Processes.process="*add*") OR (Processes.process_name=netsh.exe Processes.process="*advfirewall*" Processes.process="*3389*") OR (Processes.process_name=reg.exe Processes.process="*fDenyTSConnections*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Reverse SSH tunnel to OkoBot infrastructure from user endpoint AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the TookPS SSH tunnel: sshd.exe making outbound public connections (reverse tunnel) from a workstation, or ssh/sshd reaching OkoBot's confirmed bot IPs 104.243.43.16, 104.243.32.213, 62.210.188.209. SSH daemon egress from an endpoint is abnormal. Rationale: The three SSH-bot IPs are from Securelist's IOC list; sshd.exe egress is the reverse-tunnel behaviour the article describes (forwarding local RDP over SSH). Endpoint SSH daemon outbound is inherently rare. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running an SSH reverse tunnel legitimately (e.g. remote dev access) — check user role
  • IT using OpenSSH server on a jump host
  • Automated backup/replication over SSH from a server (not a workstation)
  • CI runner establishing SSH to a build host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is sshd.exe (daemon egressing = tunnel) and resolve the remote IP; match against the three bot IPs. 2) Contain: kill ssh/sshd, delete %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\go.bat and the 'Apple Sync' task, block the IPs at egress, isolate host. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts beaconing to the same IPs and check for the RDP-enablement chain and OkoBot staging files.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sshd.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ssh.exe","sshd.exe") and RemoteIP in ("104.243.43.16","104.243.32.213","62.210.188.209"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("104.243.43.16","104.243.32.213","62.210.188.209")
    or (DstPortNumber == 22 and NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\sshd.exe OR *\SSHD.EXE) OR @DestinationIp:(104.243.43.16 OR 104.243.32.213 OR 62.210.188.209))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| (ContextImageFileName=/sshd\.exe$/i OR RemoteAddressIP4=/^(104\.243\.43\.16|104\.243\.32\.213|62\.210\.188\.209)$/)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where ((All_Traffic.app=sshd.exe OR All_Traffic.process_name=sshd.exe) All_Traffic.direction=outbound) OR All_Traffic.dest_ip IN (104.243.43.16,104.243.32.213,62.210.188.209) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
SeedHunter process injection into Ledger/Trezor wallet applications AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts OkoBot's SeedHunter module injecting into the Ledger Live, Ledger Wallet and Trezor Suite Electron apps — flagged as those wallet processes loading a module from Temp/AppData/ProgramData, or loading the named payloads oko.dll/seedhunter/keylog by name or MD5. Rationale: Article title + body: SeedHunter injects into Ledger Live/Ledger Wallet/Trezor Suite and hooks Electron internals; Securelist gives the injector payload names (seedhunter_x64.exe, oko.dll, keylog_x64.dll) and MD5s. Wallet apps loading modules from user-writable temp dirs is abnormal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1055.001 T1056.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wallet app auto-updater loading a freshly-downloaded module from a temp staging dir
  • Electron app loading node modules from AppData install location (tune the path filter to the vendor's real install dir)
  • EDR/AV DLL injected into the wallet process for inspection
  • Portable wallet build run from a Downloads/Temp folder by the user
Suppression filter
| where FileName !endswith ".asar" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--squirrel-update"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded module's signer/hash and its folder — legitimate Ledger/Trezor modules are signed and load from the install dir, not Temp. 2) Contain: kill the wallet process and injector, quarantine the module, isolate host, and urgently advise the user their seed phrase may be compromised — move funds using a clean device. 3) Hunt: check for moonsand.store beacon, the RC4 temp-file drop, and MC/OkoSpyware keylogger output in %TEMP% on the same host.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Ledger Live.exe","Ledger Wallet.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Ledger.exe","Trezor.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\")
    or FileName in~ ("oko.dll","seedhunter_x64.exe","keylog_x64.dll","ext_daemon.exe")
    or MD5 in~ ("dd52f5108a176c62ad807c327734ad12","70fef9fd6e351f4d53cfeee8dcdfcd99","acd31c9941b6c1cabd4e45e6877b9038","3d2b43f91f65bfbf36a9c71b6b418876")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceImageLoadEvents

Windows Defender notification suppression via registry write AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OkoBot bot silencing Defender alerts by writing Notification_Suppress / DisableNotifications / DisableEnhancedNotifications = 1 under the Windows Defender keys — a defense-evasion step it performs before staging RDP and exfil. Rationale: Article states OkoBot 'silences Defender notifications with a registry write'; the Notification_Suppress/DisableNotifications values under the Windows Defender keys are the canonical mechanism, keeping the match tightly scoped. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise GPO/Intune baseline that intentionally suppresses Defender toast notifications on managed endpoints
  • SCCM/MECM configuration baseline write
  • Admin quieting notifications on a kiosk/shared PC
  • Security-product coexistence tooling adjusting Defender UX
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","IntuneManagementExtension.exe","CcmExec.exe","omadmclient.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process — GPO/Intune agents are benign; an unsigned or user-context process is not. 2) Contain: revert the value, re-enable notifications, isolate host if the writer is untrusted. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for OkoBot staging files, 'Apple Sync' task, RDP enablement, and outbound SSH/moonsand.store traffic.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueUpdated")
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("Notification_Suppress","DisableNotifications","DisableEnhancedNotifications")
| where RegistryValueData == "1"
| where RegistryKey has "Windows Defender"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","IntuneManagementExtension.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent

| where RegistryValueData == "1"
| where RegistryKey has "Windows Defender"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Hidden Chromium extension planted via Local Extension Settings (Rilide loader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts OkoBot's Rilide loader writing into the browser 'Local Extension Settings' directory (or dropping .crx from %APPDATA%) by a non-browser process — producing extensions present on disk that never appear in the browser's extension list. Rationale: The article names 'Extensions in Local Extension Settings that never appear in the browser's extension list' and identifies Rilide as the loaded stealer; only the browser itself should write that directory, so a foreign writer is high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1176 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise extension-management tool (e.g. Chrome Browser Cloud Management helper) writing extension settings
  • Backup/sync software touching the browser profile
  • A browser helper/updater not on the allowlist writing legitimately
  • Profile-migration tooling copying user data between machines
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("CmmHelper.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and inspect the extension ID/manifest — cross-check against chrome://extensions to confirm it's hidden. 2) Contain: remove the extension directory, kill the loader, isolate host, force browser credential/session resets. 3) Hunt: look for the OkoBot dispatcher (Volume2/protobuf.dll), moonsand.store beacon, and keylogger MP4/screenshot output on the same host.

| where FolderPath has @"\Local Extension Settings\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","chrome_updater.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe","elevation_service.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

OkoBot C2 beacon to moonsand.store and TookPS/Volume2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts DNS/connections to OkoBot's confirmed C2 domains — SeedHunter's moonsand.store, Volume2's livewallpapers.online / thatwascringe.com, and TookPS's 2baserec2.guru, recavb22.online, kbeautyreviews.com, coffeesaloon.online — plus the three SSH-bot IPs. Rationale: moonsand.store is the article's stated SeedHunter C2; Securelist's IOC table supplies the corroborating TookPS/Volume2 domains and SSH-bot IPs. Exact-domain/IP matches are the highest-fidelity indicator available. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox host deliberately resolving the IOC for research
  • Security scanner probing the domains from a scanning appliance
  • DNS sinkhole/passive-DNS collector logging the lookup
  • Analyst manually browsing to the domain during triage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nslookup.exe","curl.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user; a wallet app or Volume2/protobuf.dll process reaching these is a confirmed infection. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at egress + DNS, isolate the host, and treat any hardware-wallet seed entered on it as compromised. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for any other host that resolved these domains and pivot to the SeedHunter injection, 'Apple Sync' task, and SSH tunnel detections.

let iocIPs = dynamic(["104.243.43.16","104.243.32.213","62.210.188.209"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (iocDomains) or RemoteIP in (iocIPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocDomains = dynamic(["moonsand.store","livewallpapers.online","thatwascringe.com","2baserec2.guru","recavb22.online","kbeautyreviews.com","coffeesaloon.online"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (iocDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, SrcUsername

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
