Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Creative Mail CVE-2026-3985 SQLi via checkout_uuid in cm4all REST endpoint AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated SQL injection against the Creative Mail WordPress plugin's has_checkout_consent() handler, which fails to prepare the user-supplied checkout_uuid parameter (versions <=1.6.9). A legitimate checkout_uuid is a UUID (hex + hyphens); any SQL metacharacters/keywords in that parameter indicate exploitation of CVE-2026-3985. Rationale: The parameter name checkout_uuid and the vulnerable has_checkout_consent() method are the CVE-2026-3985-specific anchors; a real checkout_uuid is a UUID so any SQL token in it is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against Wordfence threat-intel, the FreshySites bulletin and CleanTalk research confirming versions <=1.6.9, unauthenticated, param checkout_uuid. Cross-checked against: • https://freshysites.com/security-bulletins/creative-mail-easier-wordpress-woocommerce-email-marketing-plugin-vulnerability-cve-2026-3985/ • https://www.wordfence.com/threat-intel/vulnerabilities/wordpress-plugins/creative-mail-by-constant-contact • https://research.cleantalk.org/reports/app/creative-mail-by-constant-contact • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-3985
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Wordfence scan, Nessus, Acunetix, WPScan) probing the endpoint with benign SQLi test strings
  • Authorized pentest / bug-bounty testing against the WooCommerce checkout consent flow
  • WAF product self-tests that replay SQLi signatures against live routes
  • A legitimate checkout_uuid that coincidentally contains the substring 'select' or 'union' inside a longer opaque token (rare with strict UUID validation)
Suppression filter
| where not(Url matches regex @"(?i)checkout_uuid=[0-9a-f%\-]+(&|$)")   // keep only checkout_uuid values containing chars outside a valid UUID
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Creative Mail plugin + WooCommerce are installed and version <=1.6.9; inspect the full uri_query and the response status/size — HTTP 200 with varying response length across requests suggests successful blind extraction. 2) Contain: disable/deactivate the Creative Mail plugin (WordPress advises this until patched) and block the source IP at the WAF; rotate WordPress admin password hashes and any secret tokens if extraction is confirmed. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for repeated checkout_uuid requests (see companion burst UC), review DB/query logs for reads against wp_users/wp_options, and check for follow-on authenticated logins using leaked admin hashes.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "checkout_uuid"
// legit checkout_uuid is a UUID (hex + hyphens only); anything below is injection syntax
| where Url has_any ("union","select","sleep(","benchmark(","information_schema","'","--","/*!"," or ")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Creative Mail blind SQLi burst — repeated checkout_uuid requests from single source AIActions on Objectives Medium
CVE-2026-3985 is a blind SQL injection that requires many chained requests to extract data (admin password hashes and secret tokens) character-by-character. This surfaces a single source IP issuing an abnormal volume of requests carrying the checkout_uuid parameter to the Creative Mail endpoint within a short window — the tell-tale shape of blind/boolean extraction rather than a one-shot probe. Rationale: Article states exploitation 'requires multiple chained requests' and extracts admin hashes/secret tokens — a volumetric/distinct-query burst on the checkout_uuid parameter is the article-specific signature of that blind extraction, distinct from the single-shot payload UC. Thresholds (>30 requests, >15 distinct variants per 10m from one IP) tuned to boolean/time-based extraction which a normal checkout never produces. Cross-checked against: • https://freshysites.com/security-bulletins/creative-mail-easier-wordpress-woocommerce-email-marketing-plugin-vulnerability-cve-2026-3985/ • https://www.wordfence.com/threat-intel/vulnerabilities/wordpress-plugins/creative-mail-by-constant-contact
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanner sweeping many payload permutations against the endpoint
  • Load/performance testing tools hammering the checkout flow
  • A busy legitimate storefront where many genuine shoppers hit checkout consent (mitigated by requiring >15 distinct query variants from a single IP)
  • Security researcher / bug-bounty extraction PoC replayed in a test environment
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1")   // exclude loopback/health-check origins; add known scanner egress IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the flagged source IP, review the sequence of checkout_uuid values — incrementing boolean conditions or SLEEP/SUBSTRING patterns confirm blind extraction; correlate with response-size or response-time variance. 2) Contain: block the IP at the WAF/edge and deactivate the Creative Mail plugin; assume DB read occurred and rotate admin credentials + secret tokens. 3) Hunt: search auth logs for admin logins from new IPs/UA post-burst (leaked hashes cracked), review other public-facing WordPress plugins for the same source IP, and check egress for exfiltration of the extracted data.

| where Url has "checkout_uuid"
| summarize reqCount = count(), distinctQueries = dcount(Url), firstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), lastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
// blind SQLi extracts char-by-char: many requests, many distinct query variants from one IP in a short window
| where reqCount > 30 and distinctQueries > 15
| order by reqCount desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command/script interpreter — CVE-2026-56164/45659/32201 RCE · [LLM] LegacyHive EoP — cross-user UsrClass.dat mounted under another user's HKU\<SID>\_Classes
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SharePoint web shell / .aspx payload written by w3wp.exe into LAYOUTS directory

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command/script interpreter — CVE-2026-56164/45659/32201 RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts post-exploitation command execution on on-prem SharePoint Servers where the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns a shell or LOLBin. CISA flagged CVE-2026-56164, CVE-2026-45659 and CVE-2026-32201 as actively exploited for unauthenticated RCE followed by hands-on-keyboard activity — a SharePoint app-pool worker launching cmd/powershell is the canonical webshell-to-RCE tell. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated SharePoint RCE + post-exploitation chain (CVE-2026-56164/45659/32201) and the near-universally-rare w3wp.exe→interpreter parent/child pair; a SharePoint app-pool worker never legitimately launches cmd/powershell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-adds-four-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-admins-to-patch-actively-exploited-sharepoint-flaws/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sharepoint-rce-cve-2026-45659-added-to.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health jobs invoking PSConfig via a custom app pool during patch/PSConfig runs
  • Admin-authored SharePoint solution deployments (stsadm/Add-SPSolution) that shell out
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM/Nagios) configured to run scripts under the IIS identity
  • Legitimate custom web parts that call certutil for certificate operations
  • Backup/AV products briefly hosting under w3wp during scans
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig","stsadm","Add-SPSolution","Install-SPFeature") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "SharePoint")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; confirm the host is an on-prem SharePoint server (2016/2019/SE) and whether it is internet-facing. Check IIS logs for a preceding unauthenticated POST to /_layouts/ endpoints around the process time. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and take w3wp offline; block the source IP at the edge. 3) HUNT: Search DeviceFileEvents for .aspx/.ashx dropped by w3wp (webshell), and pivot to machine-key theft — treat ASP.NET machineKey as compromised and rotate it, since a stolen key survives patching.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint web shell / .aspx payload written by w3wp.exe into LAYOUTS directory AIInstallation High
Hunts persistence following SharePoint RCE where the IIS worker w3wp.exe writes a web-accessible .aspx/.ashx/.asmx file into the SharePoint LAYOUTS / Web Server Extensions tree. The article states attackers used these SharePoint flaws to steal IIS machine keys and deploy malware for persistence; an IIS worker writing script files into its own web root is the classic web-shell drop. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit post-exploitation behaviours (machine-key theft, deserialization, malware deploy for persistence) mapped to the highest-fidelity SharePoint web-shell artifact: an IIS worker writing server-side script into the LAYOUTS web root, which never happens in normal operation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-admins-to-patch-actively-exploited-sharepoint-flaws/ • https://www.securityweek.com/cisa-urges-immediate-patching-of-exploited-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1606.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint solution/feature deployment (WSP) that provisions .aspx application pages
  • Cumulative-update/PSConfig runs staging new layouts pages
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in installers writing application pages under LAYOUTS
  • Admin manually copying a custom application page via an authenticated content-deployment job
  • Backup/restore of the hive/site collection that re-materializes .aspx files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig","owstimer","SPUCWorkerProcess") or FolderPath has @"\CONFIG\Upgrade\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve and read the written file — confirm whether it contains eval/Request/Process web-shell code vs a signed vendor page; check its SHA256 against known-good SharePoint pages and note the writing w3wp identity. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the file, isolate the server, and rotate the ASP.NET machineKey immediately (a stolen key lets the attacker forge auth even after patching). 3) HUNT: Search DeviceNetworkEvents for the source IP hitting the new page path, and DeviceProcessEvents for w3wp→interpreter execution proving hands-on-keyboard use of the shell.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", "Web Server Extensions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "w3wp.exe"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx","ashx","asmx")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", "Web Server Extensions")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SharePoint Web Shell Written by IIS Worker to LAYOUTS Directory
id: 2f9c4d17-8a63-4b0e-91d2-7e5a3c9b6d40
description: Detects w3wp.exe writing an .aspx/.ashx/.asmx file into the SharePoint LAYOUTS / Web Server Extensions tree, a web-shell persistence artifact of CVE-2026-56164/45659/32201 exploitation.
references:

  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-admins-to-patch-actively-exploited-sharepoint-flaws/

| TargetFileName=/\.(aspx|ashx|asmx)$/i
| regex("(?i)(\\\\TEMPLATE\\\\LAYOUTS\\\\|\\\\Web Server Extensions\\\\)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName], function=count())

LegacyHive EoP — cross-user UsrClass.dat mounted under another user's HKU\<SID>\_Classes AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the LegacyHive (Nightmare-Eclipse) Windows User Profile Service arbitrary-hive-load zero-day, where a standard-user process steers a profile load so one user's UsrClass.dat is mounted under a DIFFERENT user's HKU\<SID>\_Classes namespace. Detects registry value writes into a _Classes hive whose SID does not match the initiating process's own SID — the highest-confidence redirection indicator for this exploit. Rationale: Built from the corroborated LegacyHive mechanics (offline hive edit + Object Manager symlink + synchronized profile load) using the article/Cyderes-confirmed tell — a UsrClass.dat mounted under another user's HKU\<SID>\_Classes — expressed as a cross-SID registry-write comparison that surfaces the mismatched SID at runtime (no placeholder). Sigma/Datadog/Falcon left empty because the detection requires comparing two fields (writer SID vs key-path SID), which those single-selection/no-field-comparison query surfaces cannot express. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/legacyhive-windows-user-profile-loading-vulnerability • https://cybersecuritynews.com/legacyhive-windows-0-day-vulnerability/ • https://securityonline.info/legacyhive-windows-exploit/ • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/15/microsofts-serial-tormentor-drops-legacyhive-0-day/5271723
ATT&CKT1068 T1112 T1134
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Roaming/mandatory profile provisioning where ProfSvc (SYSTEM) loads another user's classes hive — excluded by the SYSTEM/service-SID filter
  • Terminal Server / Citrix multi-session hosts where profile tooling touches many user hives under a service context
  • FSLogix / UPM profile-container mounts operating under a machine or service account (machine-account filter)
  • Backup agents enumerating user hives
  • Fast-user-switching or runas scenarios where an admin legitimately loaded a colleague's hive for troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","frxsvc.exe","frxccd.exe","UserProfileService.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\FSLogix\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the initiating process is a Medium/Low integrity standard-user process (not ProfSvc/SYSTEM) and that KeySid belongs to a different, higher-privileged account; inspect the parent chain for a suspended benign binary (notepad.exe) launched via CreateProcessWithLogonW. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, suspend the standard user's sessions, and force a password reset for both the attacker-supplied standard account and the targeted (often admin) account. 3) HUNT: Look on the same host for NTUSER.DAT offline modification of the Local AppData value and Object Manager symlink creation under \BaseNamedObjects\Restricted; review DeviceProcessEvents for any SYSTEM-context children spawned by the standard user shortly after.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has "_Classes"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountSid !in ("S-1-5-18","S-1-5-19","S-1-5-20")
| where InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel in ("Medium","Low")
| extend KeySid = extract(@"(S-1-5-21-[0-9\-]+)_Classes", 1, RegistryKey)
| where isnotempty(KeySid)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountSid != KeySid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountSid,
          KeySid, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4657
| where ObjectName has "_Classes"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where SubjectUserSid !in ("S-1-5-18","S-1-5-19","S-1-5-20")
| extend KeySid = extract(@"(S-1-5-21-[0-9\-]+)_Classes", 1, ObjectName)
| where isnotempty(KeySid)
| where SubjectUserSid != KeySid
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectUserSid, KeySid, ObjectName, ObjectValueName, ProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*_Classes*" AND Registry.user!="SYSTEM" AND Registry.user!="*$" by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.process_name Registry.registry_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | rex field=registry_path "(?<KeySid>S-1-5-21-[0-9\-]+)_Classes" | where isnotnull(KeySid) | eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%F %T") | table firstTime dest user process_name KeySid registry_path count | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*_Classes*" AND Registry.user!="SYSTEM" AND Registry.user!="*$" by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.process_name Registry.registry_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | rex field=registry_path "(?<KeySid>S-1-5-21-[0-9\-]+)_Classes" | where isnotnull(KeySid) | eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%F %T") | table firstTime dest user process_name KeySid registry_path count | sort - firstTime

Critical

Cursor Flaw Lets Malicious Cloned Repositories Trigger Windows Code Execution

The Hacker News
2026-07-15 7 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Open a repository in Cursor&nbsp;on Windows and, if a file named&nbsp;git.exe&nbsp;is sitting in the project root, Cursor runs it. No click, no approval dialog, no warning that anything in the folder is about to execute. Whatever that binary does, it does as you, with your source, your SSH keys and your cloud tokens. Cursor keeps re-running it for as long as the project stays open. No prompt

AI IDE runs workspace-root git.exe via 'rev-parse --show-toplevel' probe (Cursor search-order RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact Cursor 0-day mechanism: an AI coding IDE (Cursor/Codex/Gemini/Kiro) spawning a git.exe that lives OUTSIDE a standard Git install directory while issuing the repository-root probe 'git rev-parse --show-toplevel'. The real git ships from Program Files\Git; a git.exe running from a cloned-repo root is an attacker-planted binary executing as the user on folder-open. Rationale: Anchors on the article's ProcMon evidence: Cursor.exe spawning a repo-root binary with 'git rev-parse --show-toplevel'. The discriminator is a git.exe whose image path is not a legitimate Git install dir — the real git ships from Program Files\Git, so a planted one lights up immediately. Cross-checked against: • https://mindgard.ai/blog/cursor-0day-when-full-disclosure-becomes-the-only-protection-left • https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/cursor-ide-malicious-code-poisoned-repos • https://www.securityweek.com/unpatched-cursor-vulnerability-exposes-users-to-code-execution/
ATT&CKT1203 T1574.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately installs git portable into a project/tools subfolder and the IDE resolves it there
  • Scoop/portable Git installs under a non-standard user path not covered by the exclusion list
  • Custom developer tooling that wraps git.exe in a repo-local bin directory
  • Monorepo bootstrap scripts that vendor a pinned git.exe for reproducible builds
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has @"\tools\" or FolderPath has @"\.bin\") | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\bootstrap\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FolderPath/SHA256 of the git.exe. Legit git is signed by 'Johannes Schindelin/Git for Windows' from Program Files\Git — an unsigned or user-path git.exe under a cloned repo root is malicious. Identify the repo and its clone origin. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, quarantine the repo folder, and rotate any credentials/SSH keys/cloud tokens accessible to the logged-on user (the payload runs as them). 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for git.exe/node.exe/npx.exe/where.exe executing from user repo dirs (UC2); review the user's recent git clone history and other opened workspaces for the same planted binary hash/name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "git.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "rev-parse" and ProcessCommandLine has "--show-toplevel"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Cursor.exe","Code.exe","codex.exe","gemini.exe","kiro.exe")
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Git\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files (x86)\Git\" or FolderPath has @"\scoop\apps\git\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\git.exe"
| where CommandLine has "rev-parse" and CommandLine has "--show-toplevel"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Cursor.exe","Code.exe","codex.exe","gemini.exe","kiro.exe")
| where not(NewProcessName has "\\Program Files\\Git\\" or NewProcessName has "\\Program Files (x86)\\Git\\" or NewProcessName has "\\scoop\\apps\\git\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects an AI coding IDE spawning a git.exe located outside a standard Git install directory while running the 'git rev-parse --show-toplevel' probe, indicating execution of an attacker-planted git.exe from a cloned repository root.

AI IDE spawns helper binary (git/node/npx/where.exe) from cloned-repo root AIDelivery High
Broadens the Cursor class across Copilot/Gemini/Codex/Kiro and the four named binaries. Cymulate: 'git.exe, npx.exe, node.exe, and where.exe have no business in a project root.' Flags any of these executing from a user workspace path (Downloads, source\repos, Desktop, OneDrive) while parented by an AI IDE — the search-order/working-directory hijack landing a malicious binary on folder-open. Rationale: Uses Cymulate's exact IOC list (git.exe/npx.exe/node.exe/where.exe 'have no business in a project root') plus the AI-IDE parent set and a user-workspace path predicate — the precise shape of the search-order hijack across all four affected vendors. Cross-checked against: • https://cymulate.com/blog/the-race-to-ship-ai-tools-left-security-behind-part-1-sandbox-escape/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019f60be-331e-74a7-b2d0-5e9cac5915eb • https://gbhackers.com/ai-developer-tools/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002 T1574.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js project legitimately shipping a vendored node.exe in a tools/ subdir opened in VS Code
  • nvm-for-windows shims not fully covered by the exclusion (add the specific nvm path)
  • Electron/build tooling that copies node.exe into a build output folder inside the repo
  • where.exe invoked by a repo build script that the IDE terminal launched
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build" | where not(FolderPath has @"\node_modules\" or FolderPath has @"\tools\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary's signer and hash. A signed Node.js/Git binary from a vendored tools dir is likely benign; an unsigned exe matching one of these names in Downloads/source\repos is not. Check the repo's remote origin. 2) Contain: terminate the process, isolate the host, quarantine the repo, and rotate user-scoped secrets (SSH keys, cloud tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 across the fleet, review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from that PID, and check whether the same repo was opened on other developer machines.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe","node.exe","npx.exe","where.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Cursor.exe","Code.exe","codex.exe","gemini.exe","kiro.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\source\repos\", @"\Desktop\", @"\OneDrive\", @"\Documents\", @"\repos\", @"\Projects\")
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Program Files\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files (x86)\" or FolderPath has @"\System32\" or FolderPath has @"\nvm\" or FolderPath has @"\scoop\apps\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\git.exe","\\node.exe","\\npx.exe","\\where.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Cursor.exe","Code.exe","codex.exe","gemini.exe","kiro.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\Downloads\\","\\source\\repos\\","\\Desktop\\","\\OneDrive\\","\\Documents\\","\\repos\\","\\Projects\\")
| where not(NewProcessName has "\\Program Files\\" or NewProcessName has "\\System32\\" or NewProcessName has "\\nvm\\" or NewProcessName has "\\scoop\\apps\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloned-repo Git hook executes shell via IDE/git subprocess (Cursor CVE-2026-26268 class) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts execution originating from a repository's .git\hooks directory — the vector behind Cursor's Git-hook sandbox escape (CVE-2026-26268). Surfaces interpreters/binaries whose image path or command line references .git\hooks and are launched by git.exe or an AI IDE, indicating a poisoned hook auto-firing during clone/checkout in an opened workspace. Rationale: Anchors on the .git\hooks path referenced in the article's disclosure timeline for Cursor's Git-hook sandbox escape (CVE-2026-26268, GHSA-8pcm-8jpx-hv8r). Ties hook execution to a git or IDE parent to raise fidelity above generic hook noise. Cross-checked against: • https://mindgard.ai/blog/cursor-0day-when-full-disclosure-becomes-the-only-protection-left • https://www.securityweek.com/unpatched-cursor-vulnerability-exposes-users-to-code-execution/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Husky/lint-staged pre-commit and pre-push hooks firing on normal commits
  • Legitimate CI-style post-checkout hooks running formatters or codegen
  • Developer-installed global core.hooksPath tooling
  • commit-msg hooks invoking node/python linters in the repo
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "husky" or ProcessCommandLine has "lint-staged" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "husky")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the hook file referenced (.git/hooks/pre-commit, post-checkout, etc.) and read its contents; benign hooks are husky/lint-staged wrappers, malicious ones fetch/exec external payloads or drop binaries. Correlate with a recent clone of an untrusted repo. 2) Contain: if the hook body is hostile, kill the process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the repo; rotate user secrets. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for egress from the hook process, review other repos on the host for identical hook hashes, and check whether Cursor is below the 2.5 fixed version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\.git\hooks\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\.git\hooks\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\.git\hooks\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("git.exe","Cursor.exe","Code.exe","codex.exe","gemini.exe","kiro.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "\\.git\\hooks\\" or CommandLine has "\\.git\\hooks\\"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git.exe","Cursor.exe","Code.exe","codex.exe","gemini.exe","kiro.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Poisoned .vscode/tasks.json lands in cloned repo via git/archive (AWS Kiro CVE-2026-10591) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a .vscode\tasks.json file being written into a workspace by a clone/extract process (git.exe, curl, tar, node) rather than an interactive editor — the delivery step of the Kiro agent file-write flaw (CVE-2026-10591) where a poisoned tasks.json auto-executes on folder-open. Fixed in Kiro 0.11, which now requires approval to modify execution-sensitive paths. Rationale: Targets the exact Kiro vector the article describes — a poisoned .vscode/tasks.json auto-executing on folder open (CVE-2026-10591, patched in Kiro 0.11). Filtering on a clone/extract writer (not an editor) distinguishes attacker-delivered config from a developer editing their own tasks.json. Cross-checked against: • https://cymulate.com/blog/the-race-to-ship-ai-tools-left-security-behind-part-1-sandbox-escape/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019f60be-331e-74a7-b2d0-5e9cac5915eb
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate git clone of a trusted internal repo that genuinely contains a .vscode/tasks.json
  • tar/7z extraction of a project template that ships a workspace config
  • node-based scaffolding tools (create-*, yo) generating .vscode/tasks.json
  • Repo sync tooling restoring workspace settings
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("github.com","dev.azure.com") == false or FolderPath has @"\Downloads\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the delivered tasks.json — inspect the command/args and the 'runOptions.runOn' field; 'folderOpen' auto-run plus a shell/download command is malicious. Identify the source repo/archive. 2) Contain: if hostile, isolate the host, quarantine the repo, and block folder-open auto-run; ensure Kiro is on 0.11+ which requires approval for tasks.json changes. 3) Hunt: correlate this file-write with any child shell (cmd/powershell) spawned by Kiro.exe/Code.exe shortly after, and sweep other developer hosts that cloned the same repo.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tasks.json"
| where FolderPath has @"\.vscode\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","curl.exe","tar.exe","node.exe","7z.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tasks.json"
| where TargetFilePath has "\\.vscode\\"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git.exe","curl.exe","tar.exe","node.exe","7z.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] IoT Telnet/ADB brute-force scanner fan-out (Akiru propagation) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TuxBot v3 Evolution sample execution by SHA256 · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — TuxBot v3: Inside an IoT Botnet Framework With LLM-Assisted Development
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TuxBot/Akiru C2 & dropper connection (209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127) · [LLM] DNS/HTTP resolution of TuxBot developer domain digikalas.online · [LLM] TuxBot bot-protocol beacon on TCP/31337 to public host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TuxBot/Akiru C2 & dropper connection (209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to TuxBot v3 Evolution's confirmed command-and-control server (209.182.237.133, SSH banner SSH-2.0-CNC-Control-Server on TCP/2222) and the Keksec/Kaitori shared dropper host 185.10.68.127. Any internal host — especially a Linux/IoT device — reaching these IPs indicates active infection or beaconing. Rationale: Anchored on the two IOCs Unit 42 and The Hacker News both attribute to TuxBot: 209.182.237.133:2222 (SSH-2.0-CNC-Control-Server, first seen on Xpanse 2026-03-05) and the FlokiNET-hosted dropper 185.10.68.127 serving Kaitori v3.9 — fixed infrastructure, near-zero legitimate reason to contact. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html • https://community.gurucul.com/articles/ThreatResearch/TuxBot-v3-Evolution-Akiru-Framework-1-6-2026 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/

TuxBot v3 Evolution sample execution by SHA256 AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the known TuxBot x86_64 debug build (SHA256 71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d, submitted to VirusTotal 2026-01-20 with symbols). Direct hash match confirms the Akiru bot agent ran on an endpoint. Rationale: Uses the single confirmed sample hash from the development timeline (Jan 20, 2026 VirusTotal submission, x86_64 debug build with symbols) — a hash match is unambiguous, though production builds compiled with GCC 14.2.0 will differ, hence pairing with the behavioural UCs. IoT Telnet/ADB brute-force scanner fan-out (Akiru propagation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single internal host making high-fan-out outbound connections to Telnet (23/2323) and Android Debug Bridge (5555) across many distinct public IPs — the TuxBot bot agent's confirmed working infection vector using its 1,496 Telnet credential pairs plus SSH/HTTP/ADB scanners. Rationale: Grounded in the article's statement that the Telnet scanner with 1,496 credential pairs is the one fully-working infection vector, plus the confirmed SSH/HTTP/ADB scanners; port 5555 (ADB) and 23/2323 (Telnet/Mirai-alt) fan-out from one host is a classic Mirai-lineage worming signature. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) sweeping the estate
  • IT asset-discovery / network-inventory tooling probing Telnet/ADB
  • Legitimate ADB debugging farm or CI device lab hitting many 5555 endpoints
  • Network monitoring appliance performing reachability checks
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.10.20.5") // add approved vuln-scanner / asset-discovery source IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the scanning host and whether it is an approved scanner (check source subnet against the authorized-scanner allowlist) and the initiating process. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and block outbound 23/2323/5555 at egress. 3) Hunt: on a confirmed compromise, pivot to C2 IPs (UC1), sample hash (UC2), and TCP/31337 bot protocol (UC5); review whether any scanned targets subsequently beacon.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemotePort in (23, 2323, 5555)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // mass Telnet/ADB scanning; bot brute-forces 1,496 cred pairs across many hosts
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (23, 2323, 5555)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, SourceHostName
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // mass Telnet/ADB scan fan-out
| order by DistinctTargets desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=23 OR RemotePort=2323 OR RemotePort=5555)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true))
| _count > 100
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
DNS/HTTP resolution of TuxBot developer domain digikalas.online AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS queries or HTTP connections to the TuxBot developer/operator domain digikalas.online and its subdomains (e.g. newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online), registered via Namecheap with Withheld-for-Privacy and resolving to Iran's Arvan Cloud CDN — used across the framework's build and fallback-C2 infrastructure. Rationale: digikalas.online is the operator's registered domain (Aug 6, 2025, Withheld for Privacy ehf, Arvan Cloud) and its subdomain newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online leaked in the MHDDoS Git log; a wildcard host-match catches both the leaked dev host and any fallback-C2 subdomains. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform auto-resolving the IOC for enrichment
  • Analyst manually browsing the domain during investigation
  • DNS logging appliance replaying a passive-DNS feed
  • Typosquat lookalike unrelated to the actor (verify exact domain)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR IOC-enrichment resolvers
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host and initiating process; confirm the query is exactly digikalas.online (not a benign lookalike) and whether it resolved. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domain at DNS, isolate the host if the query originated from an application process rather than a browser. 3) Hunt: pivot the host to C2 IP contact (UC1), sample hash (UC2), and Telnet/ADB scanning (UC3); add the resolved Arvan Cloud IP to watchlists.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "digikalas.online"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "digikalas.online"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TuxBot bot-protocol beacon on TCP/31337 to public host AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound TCP connections to port 31337 — the bot-protocol port hard-coded in the analyzed TuxBot build's encrypted C2 channel. Lower-fidelity than the IP/hash UCs because the port is operator-configurable, so scoped as a per-host beaconing hunt. Rationale: The analyzed development build set the bot protocol port to 31337 (with C2 at loopback 127.0.0.1); the port is a concrete, article-stated value but modifiable in production, so this is framed as a hunting-tier per-host beacon rather than an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1571 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy/CTF or 'elite'-port test services intentionally bound to 31337
  • Back Orifice-era honeypot or deception tooling listening on 31337
  • Custom internal application coincidentally using port 31337
  • Pentest C2 framework in an authorized engagement
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pentest-c2.exe") // exclude sanctioned red-team tooling by process name
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, initiating process, and destination IP; check whether the destination overlaps the known C2 IPs (UC1) or resolves from digikalas.online (UC4). 2) Contain: if the process is not an approved application, isolate the host and block 31337 egress. 3) Hunt: correlate with Telnet/ADB scanning (UC3) and the sample hash (UC2) on the same host; profile beacon regularity to confirm C2 rather than one-off.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 31337
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Targets = make_set(RemoteIP, 10) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Count desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 31337
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Targets = make_set(DestinationIP, 10) by SourceIP, SourceHostName
| order by Count desc

| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| order by conn_count desc

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

DeviceProcessEvents

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot 'Apple Sync' scheduled task maintaining reverse SSH-over-RDP tunnel AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a scheduled task literally named 'Apple Sync' that OkoBot's SSH bot registers to re-establish a reverse SSH tunnel forwarding the local RDP port every hour. This is a unique, framework-specific persistence + C2-maintenance artifact. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim task name 'Apple Sync' (article code block + corroborated by Securelist/TheHackerNews); a fixed, non-generic string with essentially no legitimate use, making it a high-fidelity alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Apple/iTunes/iCloud sync helper task (Apple's tasks use different names such as 'AppleSoftwareUpdate' — verify exact string and command action)
  • MDM/RMM tooling deploying a task that coincidentally contains the words Apple Sync
  • Analyst red-team emulating OkoBot in an authorized exercise
  • Backup software creating an hourly task with an ssh action
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppleSoftwareUpdate","MobileDeviceService") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","AppleSoftwareUpdate.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (schtasks /query /tn "Apple Sync" /xml) and confirm it launches ssh.exe with -R remote port forwarding to an external host. 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, kill the ssh.exe tunnel process, and block the destination IP at the firewall; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo\HDUtil.exe, a patched termsrv.dll, and additions to the 'Remote Desktop Users' group across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Apple Sync"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","ssh","-R")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Apple Sync"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot termsrv.dll patch for concurrent multi-session RDP AIInstallation High
Detects replacement/modification of the system library C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll by a process other than Windows servicing components. OkoBot swaps in a patched termsrv.dll to permit multiple concurrent RDP sessions on the victim. Rationale: System32\termsrv.dll is only legitimately written by Windows servicing (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker); any other writer patching it is the exact multi-RDP evasion Securelist describes and independently reported against the same TTP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://www.cryptika.com/cloud-atlas-apt-group-modifies-termsrv-dll-to-enable-multiple-rdp-sessions-on-victim-hosts/
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows cumulative/feature update replacing termsrv.dll via TrustedInstaller (excluded by the process filter)
  • Legitimate 3rd-party 'RDP Wrapper' installs by IT for multi-session labs
  • Disk imaging/restore tools rewriting system files during recovery
  • Security product self-protection rollback restoring the file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\WinSxS\" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "drvinst.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the on-disk termsrv.dll hash/version against the OS build's Microsoft-signed baseline and confirm the writing process is not a servicing component. 2) Contain: restore the original signed termsrv.dll (sfc /scannow or WinSxS restore), disable RDP if not required, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for the 'Apple Sync' task, new members of 'Remote Desktop Users', inbound-RDP firewall rules, and HDUtil.exe on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe","MsMpEng.exe","msmpeng.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\System32\"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername

OkoBot HDUtil launcher execution from %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo with 'target' deploy command AIInstallation High
Detects the VMProtect-packed OkoBot launcher HDUtil.exe running from %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo, or any child it spawns via its 'target'/'nouac'/'noattach' module-deployment commands. HDUtil is the framework's payload dispatcher. Rationale: HDUtil.exe and its fixed install path %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo\HDUtil.exe are named IOCs (Securelist + TheHackerNews); the binary name and directory have no legitimate software counterpart, and pivoting on its children surfaces every deployed module. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1059 T1105 T1480
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign in-house utility coincidentally named HDUtil.exe (verify signer and path — legitimate ones will not sit in %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo)
  • Hard-drive vendor diagnostic tools using a similar name (validate publisher signature)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • Renamed/allow-listed admin tool in the HDVideo path (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary is unsigned/VMProtect-packed and located under %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo; capture its command line for 'target'/'nouac' arguments and check for %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, quarantine HDUtil.exe and any child payloads (e.g. extl.exe), and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all children of HDUtil across the fleet and pivot to the C2 domain moonsand[.]store and the 'Apple Sync' task.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HDUtil.exe"
    or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe"
    or FolderPath has @"\HDVideo\"
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\HDVideo\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "HDUtil.exe"
    or ParentProcessName has "HDUtil.exe"
    or TargetProcessName has @"\HDVideo\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot UAC bypass via auto-elevated msconfig.exe spawning child process AIExploitation Medium
Detects the OkoBot 'nouac' technique in which the auto-elevated, Microsoft-signed msconfig.exe is abused (via a Windows RPC/COM elevation trick) to launch a payload at High integrity. Legitimate msconfig rarely spawns child processes. Rationale: The article names msconfig.exe as the auto-elevated binary abused for stealthy UAC bypass (Project Zero 2019 technique); msconfig spawning any non-conhost child at High integrity is an anomalous, article-specific privesc signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1548.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually opening msconfig and clicking 'Launch' on a startup/service item
  • msconfig used to relaunch services.msc or other MMC snap-ins during troubleshooting
  • Software installers that shell out to msconfig for boot configuration
  • Help-desk remote sessions running system configuration utilities
Suppression filter
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("High","System") and FolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" and FolderPath !has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process (image path, signer, integrity level) and confirm it is unsigned/from a suspicious path rather than an interactive admin action. 2) Contain: kill the elevated child, quarantine its image, and isolate if the child matches OkoBot modules (extl.exe, HDUtil.exe). 3) Hunt: correlate with a preceding HDUtil 'target nouac' command line and Defender-notification-disabling registry writes on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msconfig.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Child = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "msconfig.exe"
| where TargetProcessName !has "conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessIntegrityLevel, ParentProcessCommandLine
