OkoBot extl.exe browser-extension injector deploying Rilide Chromium stealer AIInstallation High
Detects execution of OkoBot's extl.exe injector — deployed via 'HDUtil.exe target extl.exe' — which sideloads the Rilide Chromium stealer to harvest crypto-wallet browser extension data. Targets the specific injector binary and its HDUtil parentage. Rationale: extl.exe is the named browser-extension injector and the 'HDUtil.exe target extl.exe' command is quoted verbatim; both are unique OkoBot strings tied to the Rilide Chromium wallet-extension stealer confirmed by TheHackerNews. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1176 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated internal tool named extl.exe (verify signer/path)
  • Legitimate enterprise browser-extension management deploying policies
  • Chromium developer tooling loading unpacked extensions during testing
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Google")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm extl.exe is unsigned and, if present, inspect the browser's Local Extension Settings / Extensions folders for unauthorized Rilide artifacts. 2) Contain: kill extl.exe, remove the injected extension, quarantine binaries, and force-reset affected browser profiles. 3) Hunt: check for crypto-wallet access (Ledger/Trezor/Exodus/MetaMask) and exfil to moonsand[.]store from the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "extl.exe"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "extl")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "extl.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "extl.exe"
    or (ParentProcessName has "HDUtil.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "extl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot C2 beacon to moonsand[.]store / reverse SSH tunnel egress AICommand & Control High
Detects endpoint connections resolving or connecting to the OkoBot C2 domain moonsand[.]store, or ssh.exe establishing an outbound reverse tunnel (-R remote forwarding) to a public host — the framework's SFTP module-delivery and RDP-forwarding channel. Rationale: moonsand[.]store is a discrete C2 IOC surfaced by TheHackerNews's OkoBot write-up; combined with ssh.exe reverse-tunnel (-R) egress it covers both the DNS/HTTP and SSH channels the framework uses for SFTP module delivery. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin using ssh.exe -R for authorized reverse tunneling (verify the .ssh\go.bat and destination)
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or researcher resolving moonsand[.]store for analysis
  • Security proxy/DNS-inspection appliance pre-resolving flagged domains
  • Web-content scanner crawling the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that resolved moonsand[.]store or ran ssh.exe -R and confirm the destination is attacker-controlled (check %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\go.bat). 2) Contain: block moonsand[.]store and the SSH destination IP at egress, kill the ssh.exe tunnel, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for moonsand[.]store, and on hits pivot to HDUtil.exe, the 'Apple Sync' task, and patched termsrv.dll.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "moonsand.store"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-R" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "moonsand.store"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName

OkoBot RDP enablement: user added to 'Remote Desktop Users' + inbound-RDP firewall rule AIInstallation Medium
Detects the OkoBot SSH bot's graphical-session setup: adding a local account to the 'Remote Desktop Users' group, opening inbound RDP via netsh firewall, and/or clearing fDenyTSConnections — the precursor to its multi-session RDP access. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit back-connection steps (open inbound-RDP firewall ports, add a user to 'Remote Desktop Users'); grouping the three commands raises fidelity above any single admin action. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1562.004 T1136.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT enabling RDP on a workstation for legitimate remote support
  • GPO/Intune configuration scripts opening RDP firewall rules
  • Sysadmin adding a helpdesk account to Remote Desktop Users
  • Server provisioning automation clearing fDenyTSConnections
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","IntuneManagementExtension.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "MDM"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/account and whether the change was ticketed IT activity or driven by an unknown parent (e.g. ssh.exe, HDUtil.exe). 2) Contain: revert the group membership and firewall rule, re-enable fDenyTSConnections, and isolate if unauthorized. 3) Hunt: correlate with the 'Apple Sync' task, patched termsrv.dll, and new local accounts; check for subsequent inbound RDP logons (LogonType 10).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and ProcessCommandLine has "/add")
    or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("3389","Remote Desktop","RemoteDesktop"))
    or ProcessCommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and CommandLine has "/add")
    or (NewProcessName has "netsh.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("3389","Remote Desktop","RemoteDesktop"))
    or CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot SeedHunter memory injection into cryptocurrency wallet applications AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts remote-thread/process-memory injection into desktop crypto-wallet apps (Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Exodus, Tonkeeper) — the mechanism OkoBot's SeedHunter/OkoSpyware modules use to overlay seed-phrase phishing and capture recovery phrases from wallet windows. Rationale: TheHackerNews confirms SeedHunter injects seed-phrase phishing into Ledger and Trezor apps; hunting cross-process injection into these named wallet binaries targets the collection mechanism directly. Sentinel left empty because the canonical tenant schema lacks an API-call/injection table (DeviceEvents is not onboarded); use Defender/Falcon or Sysmon EID 8/10. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1055 T1113
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate security/EDR agents reading wallet-app memory for scanning
  • Wallet auto-updaters or crash-reporters accessing their own process (excluded by self-filter)
  • Accessibility/overlay tools (screen readers, password managers) hooking wallet windows
  • Debuggers used by a wallet developer on the endpoint
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Microsoft Corporation","CrowdStrike, Inc.") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the injector process (path, signer) accessing the wallet app; confirm it is not the wallet's own updater or an EDR agent. 2) Contain: kill the injector, quarantine its binary, and advise the user their seed phrase may be compromised — move funds from a clean device. 3) Hunt: link to HDUtil.exe/extl.exe, OkoSpyware/MC Keylogger artifacts, and exfil to moonsand[.]store on the host and any wallets accessed from it.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall","QueueUserApcRemoteApiCall")
| where FileName in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType,
          TargetApp = FileName,
          Injector = InitiatingProcessFileName, InjectorPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InjectorCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall","QueueUserApcRemoteApiCall")
| where FileName in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType,
          TargetApp = FileName,
          Injector = InitiatingProcessFileName, InjectorPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InjectorCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Install of compromised @asyncapi npm package versions (generator/helpers/components/specs) AIDelivery High
Hunts for developer or CI hosts installing the specific poisoned @asyncapi package versions published on 2026-07-14 that carry the Miasma dropper. Grounded on the exact package@version strings from the article, so it flags exposure regardless of whether the module was ever require()d. Rationale: Uses the five exact compromised package@version strings named in the article and confirmed by Socket/StepSecurity/OX Security. These versions were unpublished, so any residual reference is high-fidelity exposure evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A remediation/IR engineer intentionally installing the pinned bad version in an isolated lab to reverse it
  • An internal mirror serving a cached copy that still lists the old version in a lockfile audit command
  • Security scanner (e.g. Socket/Snyk CLI) echoing the package@version string in its own command line while auditing
  • A developer typing the version in a `npm view @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1` diagnostic command
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm view" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "audit"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host/user ran the install and whether it was a build/CI agent or a dev laptop; check DeviceProcessEvents for any node.exe child spawned shortly after. 2) Contain: isolate the host, rotate any credentials reachable from it (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS keys, SSH keys, browser sessions) and remove the package from the affected lockfile/registry cache. 3) Hunt: pivot to IPFS gateway fetches of CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9, sync.js file drops, and outbound connections to 85.137.53.71.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm") or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js spawns detached background node fetching Miasma stage-2 from IPFS gatewa AIDelivery High
Hunts the require()-time dropper behaviour where a node/npm process launches a detached child node that pulls the encrypted stage-2 (sync.js) from the IPFS gateway. Anchored on the article's IPFS CID and gateway path rather than a generic node-spawns-node pattern. Rationale: Combines the article's parent-child chain (module load -> detached node) with the exact IPFS CID/gateway path and sync.js loader name, giving a high-fidelity delivery-stage detection distinct from generic node execution. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legit IPFS-based dev tool (e.g. js-ipfs/Helia) fetching content via ipfs.io through node
  • A frontend project genuinely named sync.js being launched with node during a build
  • A developer manually curl-ing an IPFS gateway inside an npm run script for testing
  • Package tarball integrity tooling referencing an ipfs.io mirror
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9" or ProcessCommandLine has "sync.js"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child node command line and the parent lockfile/module path; confirm the CID matches QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9. 2) Contain: kill the detached node process tree, isolate the host, and block the IPFS gateway CID at proxy. 3) Hunt: look for sync.js written to temp/appdata, registry Run-key persistence written by node, and beacons to 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs.io/ipfs/","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","sync.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm")
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs.io/ipfs/","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","sync.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IPFS gateway fetch of Miasma stage-2 CID (ipfs.io/ipfs/QmQobZSp...) AIDelivery High
Network-layer detection for a host retrieving the encrypted second stage from the exact IPFS CID hosted on ipfs.io. Pivots on the CID string in the URL, which uniquely identifies this campaign's payload regardless of the fetching process. Rationale: The IPFS CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9 in the download URL is a unique campaign IOC confirmed across Socket, SafeDep and Datadog; the URL-path match is near-zero FP. DNS-only fallback (ipfs.io + node) is used where proxy telemetry is absent. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of the public ipfs.io gateway by a decentralized-app developer
  • A CI job resolving ipfs.io for an unrelated, benign CID (only the DNS fallback clause, not the CID clause)
  • Security researcher fetching the CID for analysis from a sanctioned host
  • Corporate proxy prefetch/cache warming ipfs.io
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteUrl has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URL contained the exact CID (true positive) vs a generic ipfs.io hit (needs enrichment); identify the fetching process. 2) Contain: block the CID/gateway at web proxy and isolate the host if the CID matched. 3) Hunt: correlate to the node parent chain, sync.js drop, persistence writes, and 85.137.53.71 beaconing on the same host.

   or (RemoteUrl has "ipfs.io" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession

| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent

Miasma sync.js loader dropped to OS-specific path by node and executed AIInstallation Medium
Detects the encrypted stage-2 JavaScript loader 'sync.js' being written by a node/npm process to a staging path, the precursor to Miasma tasking-framework execution. Scoped to node-parented writes plus temp/appdata/hidden-dir staging seen in the campaign. Rationale: sync.js is the article's named stage-2 loader; pairing the exact filename with a node/npm writer and the campaign's staging locations (temp/appdata/.config/.cache/node_modules per Datadog & CybersecurityNews) keeps FPs on the common filename manageable. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-turns-trusted-npm-packages-into-persistent-backdoors/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browsersync/webpack-dev-server writing a sync.js helper during a build
  • A project that legitimately ships a module named sync.js into node_modules
  • Editor autosave dropping sync.js into an AppData temp workspace
  • Test frameworks generating sync.js fixtures in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.config/.miasma", "mesa_shader_cache") or SHA256 in ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1","082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab","bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped sync.js and compare to the article SHA256 set; inspect the writing node command line and parent package. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate developer credentials if execution followed the write. 3) Hunt: check for immediate outbound to ipfs.io CID or 85.137.53.71, plus systemd/launchd/Run-key persistence created by the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\node_modules\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", "/.config/", "/.cache/", "/tmp/", "node_modules")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma botnet C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound connections from any endpoint to the confirmed Miasma C2 host 85.137.53.71 (AS43641, NL) — command server 8080, exfil 8081, proxy-mgmt 8091. IP-anchored so it fires regardless of which of the six C2 channels is used. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 is the confirmed Miasma C2 IP (StepSecurity/Rescana attribute 8080 command, 8081 exfil, 8091 proxy-mgmt on AS43641). A hard IP match with per-port summarization is a low-FP, high-severity C2 detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-asyncapi-npm-supply-chain-attack-delivers-multi-stage-miasma-botnet-via-compromised-github-act
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/IR analyst deliberately connecting to the C2 from a sanctioned sandbox for analysis
  • A shared-hosting IP reassignment where 85.137.53.71 later serves benign content (validate timestamp against disclosure date)
  • Internet-wide scanner infrastructure your org runs hitting the same IP
  • A VPN/proxy egress node coincidentally sharing the subnet (verify exact /32)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and destination port (8080/8081/8091 map to command/exfil/proxy) and whether the host imported an @asyncapi package. 2) Contain: block 85.137.53.71 at the firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and treat as data-theft (rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH creds and wallets). 3) Hunt: expand to the full IOC set — IPFS CID fetch, sync.js drop, systemd miasma-monitor.service / Run-key persistence — across all hosts that used the packages.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by FirstSeen desc

Miasma persistence via Windows Run key or startup written by node/npm process AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Windows-registry autostart persistence Miasma establishes, scoped to Run/RunOnce writes performed by a node/npm process or pointing at node/sync.js/temp staging. Complements the systemd/launchd/crontab variants on non-Windows. Rationale: The article states Miasma sets Windows Registry autostart keys (alongside systemd/launchd/crontab); scoping Run-key writes to a node/npm writer or node/sync.js/temp value data ties generic persistence telemetry to this specific dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-turns-trusted-npm-packages-into-persistent-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An Electron/Node desktop app (Slack, VS Code updater) legitimately writing a Run key that references node
  • A developer tool installer setting an autostart entry pointing into AppData
  • Squirrel/auto-updater frameworks writing RunOnce values
  • Legit npm global CLI wrappers referenced in a Run value
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Microsoft VS Code\", @"\slack\", @"\Programs\") and RegistryValueData has "--updated")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the Run value data — a path into Temp/AppData/.config or referencing sync.js/node with an odd script is the tell. 2) Contain: delete the autostart value, isolate the host, and check for the matching systemd miasma-monitor.service / launchd plist on non-Windows peers. 3) Hunt: pivot from the persisted binary to its C2 (85.137.53.71) and the IPFS stage-2 fetch across the estate.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
   or RegistryValueData has_any ("node","sync.js", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", "ProgramData")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where ActingProcessName has "node" or RegistryValueData has_any ("node","sync.js", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", "ProgramData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious downloader child (powershell/cmd/curl) spawned by npm/node_modules AIExploitation Medium
Detects a package-manager or node_modules-resident process spawning a shell/downloader with network or decode indicators — the hands-on-keyboard-free execution path of the Miasma supply-chain dropper. Scoped to node/npm/yarn/pnpm parents to avoid generic shell noise. Rationale: The dropper executes at module load inside build/CI contexts; a node/npm parent spawning a downloader shell with http/ipfs/base64/-enc indicators captures the execution pivot without the excluded generic Office-spawns-script logic. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm postinstall/build script using curl or Invoke-WebRequest to fetch a binary dependency (e.g. node-gyp, playwright browser download)
  • A CI pipeline step where node spawns powershell to run a signed installer
  • yarn/pnpm invoking cmd to run cross-platform helper scripts with URLs
  • Certutil used benignly by a build to verify a cert chain
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","playwright","puppeteer","electron") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","nodejs.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line and the parent package/script; benign build fetches usually pull vendor CDNs, not ipfs.io or base64 blobs. 2) Contain: if the URL is ipfs.io/the CID or the payload is encoded, kill the tree and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check the same host for sync.js drop, 85.137.53.71 beacon, and autostart persistence; review the CI job that triggered the install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\node_modules\"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","ipfs.io","DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","FromBase64String","-enc","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell","pwsh","cmd","curl","wget","bash","bitsadmin","certutil")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","ipfs.io","DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","FromBase64String","-enc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\npm.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\cmd.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe) @CommandLine:(*http://* OR *https://* OR *ipfs.io* OR *DownloadString* OR *Invoke-WebRequest* OR *FromBase64String* OR *-enc*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|curl|wget|bitsadmin|certutil)\.exe$/i
| regex("(https?://|ipfs\\.io|DownloadString|Invoke-WebRequest|FromBase64String|-enc)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*node_modules*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") AND (Processes.process="*http://*" OR Processes.process="*https://*" OR Processes.process="*ipfs.io*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*node_modules*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") AND (Processes.process="*http://*" OR Processes.process="*https://*" OR Processes.process="*ipfs.io*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("85.137.53.71") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["85.137.53.71"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

tags:

    product: windows

    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'

falsepositives:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web

| append

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port

| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

let BadHashes = dynamic(["34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a"]);
union

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,

                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Authentication or cloud API activity from sanctioned Media Land BPH IP 194.26.25.111 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network connection to Media Land bulletproof-hosting IP 194.26.25.111 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Network connection to Media Land bulletproof-hosting IP 194.26.25.111 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint, perimeter and cloud-network connections to/from 194.26.25.111, a Media Land BPH address named in the DOJ indictment/OFAC sanctions and independently tied to Media Land infrastructure reselling access to ransomware/Black Basta operators. Media Land hosts malware C2, ransomware data-leak sites, phishing kits and exfil servers, so any host reaching this IP is likely beaconing or staging. Rationale: Keys on the single concrete IOC in the article (194.26.25.111), confirmed as Media Land BPH infrastructure by the Disclosing.Observer data-driven reconstruction and the OFAC advisory — a direct IP match to sanctioned ransomware-hosting infra is inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0319 • https://therecord.media/us-unseals-indictment-russians-bulletproof-hosting • https://disclosing.observer/2025/11/24/bulletproof-hoster-anatomy-data-driven-reconstruction.html
ATT&CKT1071 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/malware researchers or automated sandboxes deliberately detonating samples that beacon to the IP
  • Security scanners or attack-surface-monitoring vendors probing the /24
  • A benign service that lands on the address after IP reallocation from Media Land following the takedown
  • VPN/proxy exit-node reuse of the address by an unrelated tenant
  • Blocklist/IOC-management tooling that resolves or test-connects to the IP for validation
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("sandbox-detonation-01","malware-research-vm") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("threatintel-validator.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/user and direction — is a workstation beaconing (outbound) or a server receiving (inbound)? Pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine/parent tree and any files written in the same window. 2) Contain: block 194.26.25.111 (and the surrounding 194.26.25.0/24) at firewall/proxy/EDR, isolate the host if an unsigned or LOLBin process made the connection, and reset credentials used on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for ransomware pre-cursors (shadow-copy deletion, mass file writes), search all telemetry for other Media Land ranges, and check whether any inbound admin logons preceded the connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "194.26.25.111" or LocalIP == "194.26.25.111"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, LocalPort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "194.26.25.111" or SourceIP == "194.26.25.111"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, SourceUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Network Connection to Media Land Bulletproof Hosting IP 194.26.25.111
id: 8f3c1e2a-6b4d-4a1f-9c2e-7d5b0a1f9e3c

Authentication or cloud API activity from sanctioned Media Land BPH IP 194.26.25.111 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts sign-ins, remote logons and cloud control-plane API calls sourced from 194.26.25.111, a Media Land bulletproof-hosting address under US/UK/EU sanctions. Because Media Land brokers access to ransomware and initial-access-broker operators, any valid-account authentication or AWS/Entra API call originating from this IP indicates account takeover or attacker operations from sanctioned infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the same corroborated Media Land BPH IOC (194.26.25.111) but on a distinct pivot — identity/cloud control plane rather than endpoint egress. Any valid-account or API-key use from a sanctioned bulletproof-hosting IP is a high-signal account-takeover/attacker-operations indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0319 • https://therecord.media/us-unseals-indictment-russians-bulletproof-hosting • https://disclosing.observer/2025/11/24/bulletproof-hoster-anatomy-data-driven-reconstruction.html
ATT&CKT1078 T1090.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A remote employee or contractor routing through a VPN/hosting provider that reused the address after Media Land reallocation
  • Penetration-testers or red-team operators deliberately staging from leased infrastructure in that range
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling that authenticates test accounts to observe attacker behaviour
  • Managed-service-provider automation whose egress transited a reallocated block
  • Security researchers logging into honeypot/canary tenants from the IP
Suppression filter
| where not (UserPrincipalName has_any ("redteam","pentest","canary") or AppDisplayName in~ ("Threat Intel Enrichment"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the account(s) and result type — successful sign-in or API call from 194.26.25.111 is presumed malicious; review MFA state, ClientAppUsed (legacy auth?) and what resources/APIs were touched. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and reset credentials/rotate access keys for affected identities, block the IP/range in Conditional Access and at the cloud WAF/SCP, and disable any keys used. 3) Hunt: enumerate all actions taken by the identity after the sign-in (mailbox rules, role/policy changes, data access), and search for the same IP/range across network telemetry (UC1) to find associated endpoint beaconing.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress == "194.26.25.111"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, Application, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, ErrorCode, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress == "194.26.25.111"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ResultType, ResultDescription, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA 1000 phantom /__api__/login|/__api__/logout endpoints returning HTTP 200 AIExploitation High
Hunts the primary forensic IOC SonicWall published for CVE-2026-15409/15410 exploitation: hits to /__api__/login or /__api__/logout in the SMA appliance web access log (extraweb_access.log) that return HTTP 200. SonicWall states these URIs do not exist in a legitimate SMA configuration, so any 200 response is a near-certain exploitation artifact. Rationale: Uses SonicWall's own published IOC verbatim (/__api__/login|/__api__/logout with HTTP 200) — SonicWall explicitly states these URIs are absent from legitimate config, making a 200 response an exploitation artifact rather than a probe. Cross-checked against BleepingComputer and SonicWall's product notice. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-warns-of-sma1000-flaws-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks-patch-now/ • https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) replaying the published SonicWall IOC path against the appliance for detection coverage — but these normally return 404, not 200
  • SonicWall PSIRT / support engineer validating patch efficacy by probing the endpoint on a lab appliance
  • Security team running a proof-of-concept exploit against a decommissioned/test SMA to confirm exposure
  • A reverse proxy in front of the SMA rewriting URLs such that an unrelated path collides with /__api__/ (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Rapid7"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full extraweb_access.log lines for the SrcIpAddr, confirm HTTP 200 (not 404) and capture the User-Agent and any /wsproxy hits from the same source. Check whether /var/lib/unit/conf.json now contains /__api__ routes. 2) CONTAIN: Per SonicWall guidance, isolate the appliance, re-image physical or redeploy virtual SMA, then reset ALL user and admin passwords and re-provision TOTP tokens (attackers can forge sessions). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP across firewall/VPN logs for lateral movement, review ctrl-service.log for hotfix-rollback path-traversal entries, and enumerate any accounts created or config changes made after the first 200 response.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode
| order by LastSeen desc
